documents.title: 1.1.1. Inventory Management
documents.content: Inventory Management Inventory-aware market making using Asset-Liability Management (ALM) and the Avellaneda-Stoikov framework 1. Overview AIMM uses Asset-Liability Management (ALM) inspired by Wombat Exchange and Platypus Finance: - Reserves : Actual tokens held by the pool (assets) - Liabilities : LP claims against the pool (what we owe depositors) - Coverage Ratio : This decouples pricing from reserves, enabling inventory-aware market making. 1.1. Beyond Pool-Wise Invariants Traditional AMMs (Uniswap, Curve) enforce strict pool-wise invariants (e.g., ) that don't scale well to N-asset scenarios without specialized coordinates (like polar coordinates in Balancer). AIMM replaces this with: - Per-asset tracking: Each asset maintains independent reserves and liabilities - Feedback control: Inventory skew acts as a dynamic rebalancing signal (Avellaneda-Stoikov framework) - Scalability: Naturally handles any number of assets without invariant constraints 2. Coverage Ratio 2.1. Definition $$c = \frac{R}{L}$$ where: - c = coverage ratio - R = reserves (actual tokens held) - L = liabilities (LP claims) - c = 1 (WAD scale) means 100% coverage - c 1 means overcollateralized 2.2. Key Thresholds | Coverage | State | Behavior | |----------|-------|----------| | 200%+ | Overcollateralized | Max discount (skew = -100), incentivize selling | | 100% | Equilibrium | Zero skew, normal pricing | | 50% | Critical floor | Max premium (skew = +100), withdrawal haircuts apply | | = 1$): $D = R$ (full depth = reserves) 4.4. Depth Amplifier The depth amplifier $k$ controls virtual depth addition: | Value | $k$ | Effect | |-------|-----|--------| | 0 | 0 | No amplification ($D = R$ always) | | 500000 | 0.5 | 50% max virtual addition | | 1000000 | 1.0 | 100% max virtual addition | Higher amplification = tighter spreads at low coverage, but increased risk if coverage continues dropping. 5. Withdrawal Haircut 5.1. Purpose When $c = 1$ 6.5. Parameters | Parameter | Unit | Example | |-----------|------|---------| | | 0.0001% | 980000 (98%) | | | WAD/second | ~3.17e10 (~1%/year) | See: 7. Net Coverage Impact 7.1. Purpose Determines if a swap improves or worsens pool balance. Used to apply directional fee asymmetry. 7.2. Formula $$\Delta I = I1 - I0$$ where: - ΔI = net coverage impact - I = ∑j pj × |Rj - Lj| (sum of imbalances across assets) - pj = price of asset j - Rj, Lj = reserves and liabilities of asset j - Subscripts 0, 1 = before and after trade 7.3. Interpretation | $Delta I$ | Meaning | Fee Treatment | |-----------|---------|---------------| | $ 0$ | Worsens coverage | Higher spread (toxic flow penalty) | | $= 0$ | Neutral | Base spread only | See: 8. Coverage Classification 8.1. Single Asset | Coverage | State | |----------|-------| | | OVER | | | ADEQUATE | | | UNDER | | | CRITICAL | 8.2. Pool Level Aggregate coverage across all assets: $$C = \frac{\sumj Rj \times pj}{\sumj Lj \times pj}$$ where: - C = pool-level coverage ratio - Rj = reserves of asset j - Lj = liabilities of asset j - pj = price of asset j 9. ALM Flow: Deposit 1. User deposits token $A$ 2. $RA larr RA + x$ (add to reserves) 3. $LA larr LA + x$ (1:1 LP minting) 4. Coverage remains unchanged 5. User receives LP tokens 9.1. Single-Sided Deposits ALM enables single-sided deposits — no forced pairing required. Each token's coverage ratio tracks independently. 10. ALM Flow: Withdrawal 1. User requests withdrawal of $x$ LP tokens 2. Calculate $c = R / L$ 3. If $c < 1$: - Calculate $h = (1 - c)^p$ - $y = x (1 - h)$ (apply haircut) 4. $R larr R - y$ 5. $L larr L - x$ (full LP burn) 6. User receives $y$ tokens 10.1. Cross-Asset Withdrawal User can withdraw into a different asset: 1. Burn LP tokens for token $A$ 2. Swap internal value to token $B$ 3. Apply haircut on token $B$ 4. User receives token $B$ 11. ALM Flow: Swap 1. User swaps $x$ of token $A$ for token $B$ 2. Calculate $psiA = f(cA, gamma)$ 3. Calculate $psiB = f(cB, gamma)$ 4. Price via spline traversal with skew offsets 5. $RA larr RA + x$ 6. $RB larr RB - y$ 7. Liabilities unchanged (no LP mint/burn) 8. Coverage shifts: $cA uarr$, $cB darr$ 12. Parameter Summary 12.1. Per-Asset RiskConfig | Field | Type | Unit | Purpose | |-------|------|------|---------| | | uint16 | 0.0001% | Critical coverage threshold (e.g., 500000 = 50%) | | | uint16 | 0.0001% | Decay activation threshold | | | uint32 | WAD/second | Decay rate | | | uint16 | raw (scaled by 10^6) | Virtual depth at low coverage | 12.2. Per-Asset Sensitivity | Field | Type | Unit | Purpose | |-------|------|------|---------| | | uint16 | basis 10000 | Inventory skew multiplier (10000 = 1.0x) | | | uint16 | basis 10000 | Withdrawal haircut gentleness | 13. Comparison: Traditional AMM vs AIMM ALM | Aspect | Traditional AMM | AIMM ALM | |--------|-----------------|----------| | Price source | Reserves ratio | Oracle + inventory skew | | LP tracking | Shares of pool | Specific asset liabilities | | Deposit | Both tokens required | Single-sided | | Withdrawal | Pro-rata pool share | Specific asset with haircut | | Rebalancing | Arbitrageurs only | Inventory skew incentives | | Under-collateral | Implicit (IL) | Explicit ( ) | 14. Security Considerations 14.1. Bank Run Protection 1. Haircut curve penalizes late withdrawers progressively 2. Min liquidity prevents complete drainage 3. Decay mechanism gradually restores coverage 14.2. Manipulation Resistance 1. TWAP-based pricing resists flash loan attacks 2. Skew bounds (±100) cap maximum impact 3. Coverage floor** provides hard safety boundary 14.3. Circuit Breakers - flag halts all operations - Critical coverage triggers max premium - Min liquidity requirement per asset 15. documents.title: 1.1.6. Toxic Flow Mitigation
documents.content: Anti-Toxic Flow Protection Mechanisms to mitigate adverse selection, stat-arb extraction, and JIT attacks 1. Overview AIMM is arbitrage-friendly for rebalancing but anti-toxic for extractive flows. The protocol employs multiple defense mechanisms against common AMM attack vectors while maintaining capital efficiency. For coverage ratio definition, see Inventory Management §2. Design Philosophy: - Arbitrageurs provide valuable price discovery → encouraged via fair spreads - Toxic flow extractors exploit information asymmetry → penalized via dynamic fees - Liquidity providers deserve protection from adverse selection - MEV searchers can be allies, not enemies → Cooperative MEV rebate program 2. Toxic Flow Vectors 2.1. Adverse Selection Attack: Informed traders execute against stale prices before oracle updates. Example: 1. CEX price moves ETH from $2000 → $2050 2. Trader front-runs oracle update 3. Buys ETH at $2000 from pool 4. Sells at $2050 on CEX 5. Pool LPs lose $50/ETH Impact: LPs systematically lose to informed traders. 2.2. Statistical Arbitrage vs CEXs Attack: High-frequency traders exploit price lags between pool and centralized exchanges. Characteristics: - Sub-second execution windows - Exploits oracle staleness - Unidirectional (always against LPs) - Risk-free profit extraction Impact: Continuous drain on LP returns, especially during volatile periods. 2.3. Just-In-Time (JIT) Liquidity Attack: Sophisticated actors add liquidity just before large swaps and remove immediately after, capturing fees without exposure to toxic flow. Mechanism: 1. Bot detects large pending swap in mempool 2. Adds concentrated liquidity front-running the swap 3. Captures disproportionate fee share 4. Removes liquidity in same block 5. Passive LPs bear inventory risk, JIT bot extracts fees Status: ✅ Mitigated via Flow Guard — see Flow Guards §Layer 2 The parameter (default: 15 seconds) enforces a mandatory delay between deposit→withdraw and stake→unstake operations, making atomic JIT attacks impossible. 3. AIMM Defense Mechanisms 3.1. Volatility-Based Fees Dynamic fees that increase during high volatility periods when adverse selection risk is highest. Formula Reference: See Parametrization §2.1.2 for vega formula and Internal Oracle §8 for EMA mechanics. How it protects: - Volatility spikes → fees increase automatically - Toxic flow becomes more expensive during attack windows - Arbitrageurs pay higher costs during uncertainty - LPs compensated for increased adverse selection risk 3.2. Asymmetric Spread (Deviation-Based) Prices lag true market value based on directional inventory imbalance. Higher fees charged on the imbalanced side. Formula Reference: See Parametrization §2.1.1 for skew formula and Parametrization §2.1.3 for deviation surcharge. Asymmetry: - Pool overcollateralized (selling pressure) → higher fees on buys - Pool undercollateralized (buying pressure) → higher fees on sells - Fee increases proportional to imbalance severity How it protects: - Toxic flow typically unidirectional (exploits price lag) - Imbalance indicates likely mispricing - Higher fees on imbalanced side = adverse selection protection - Rebalancing arbitrage encouraged (bringing pool back to equilibrium) 3.3. Dual-Window TWAP Oracle Internal oracle resists manipulation via dual time windows and same-block rejection. Full Documentation: See Internal Oracle for TWAP mechanics, B64 encoding, and volatility EMA implementation. How it protects: - Flash loan price manipulation → rejected (same block) - Multi-block manipulation → expensive (requires sustained capital) - Dual windows → harder to exploit both simultaneously - Volatility measured from TWAP deltas → smooths spikes 3.4. Market-Aware Bi-Factor Fee Combines protections into single adaptive fee. Full Documentation: See Spread & Fees for complete spread model and Parametrization §5 for parameter details. Adaptive behavior: - Normal conditions: ~$Sv$ (volatility band) - Oracle disagreement: +$U$ (deviation surcharge) - Coverage-worsening trades: pay $Sv + U$ - Coverage-improving trades: pay $Sv$ only (arb-friendly) 3.5. Coverage-Aware Withdrawal Haircuts Withdrawals during undercollateralization incur withdrawal haircuts, discouraging bank runs and adverse selection exits. Formula Reference: See Parametrization §2.1.4 for haircut formula and Inventory Management §5 for detailed mechanics. How it protects: - LPs can't exit at par during adverse selection events - Early exits subsidize remaining LPs - Prevents cascading withdrawals - Incentivizes staying during temporary imbalances 3.6. Cooperative Arbitrage Rather than fighting arbitrageurs, AIMM collaborates with them through a whitelisted, reputation-based rebate program that aligns incentives. The Problem with Traditional Arbitrage: - CEX-DEX arbitrageurs extract value from pools by exploiting oracle staleness - LPs bear the cost of price corrections (Loss-Versus-Rebalancing) - Adversarial relationship: arbitrageurs extract, LPs lose - No mechanism to reward arbitrageurs who help the pool AIMM's Solution: Cooperative Arbitrage: Not MEV, but Statistical Arbitrage: This mechanism targets cross-exchange (CEX-DEX) statistical arbitrage, not MEV in the formal sense (which manipulates block ordering). Cooperators are arbitrageurs—a broader category encompassing MEV searchers, HFT desks, and medium-frequency stat arb traders. How Arbitrageurs Become Cooperators: 1. Whitelist application: Arbitrageurs apply to the DAO for Cooperator status at btr.supply/coop 2. Equal starting rebate: All approved cooperators start with the same rebate tier (e.g., 20%) 3. Reputation tracking: Performance measured by 4. Tiered rebates: Higher reputation → higher rebate percentage (up to parametric max, e.g., 80%) 5. Revocation threshold: Low reputation (<0.9) leads to loss of Cooperator status 6. Competitive dynamics: All cooperators compete on equal terms; best performers earn highest rebates Parameters (pool-level governance): - : Maximum whitelisted cooperators (default: 10) - : Maximum rebate percentage (default: 8000 = 80%) - : Minimum reputation to maintain status (default: 0.9) - : Cooldown period for claiming rebates (default: 1 week) How it works: Reputation-Based Rebate Tiers: The DAO's Natural Advantage (unstated but emergent): If the DAO operates its own arbitrage bot and donates 100% of proceeds back to the pool: - Reputation = totaldonated / totalrebates → maximized - Qualifies for highest rebate tier automatically - Effectively front-runs adversarial arbitrageurs (lower profit threshold due to rebates) - Closes the LVR loop: arbitrage profits return to LPs who suffered the LVR This creates a competitive but fair game where all cooperators have equal opportunity, but those who contribute most to the pool (whether DAO or external) earn the best terms. Why this protects LPs: | Factor | Without Cooperation | With Cooperation | |--------|---------------------|------------------| | Arbitrage timing | Extract after oracle lag | Race to rebalance first (incentivized by rebates) | | Inventory impact | Extract then abandon | Actively managed (donations improve coverage) | | Price accuracy | Exploits staleness | Minimizes staleness (competitive delagging) | | LP PnL | Systematic LVR | Drastically reduced LVR (donations offset losses) | | Competition | Adversarial extraction | Cooperative improvement (reputation game) | Whitelist Rationale: - Quality control: Ensure cooperators don't expose LP deposits to excessive external CEX risk - Inventory management: DAO and trusted actors carry inventory risk (bounded to small fraction of pool TVL) - Active monitoring: Track cooperator behavior, donations, and reputation - Credit risk management: Prevent cooperators from using pool as leverage source Important: This is not fully permissionless—it requires DAO curation and monitoring. However, it avoids: - Oracle centralization (UAMM, DODO, Swaap): No single point of failure or manipulation - Manager trust (am-AMM): No single entity controlling all fees and arb profits - Builder dependency (McAMM): No reliance on off-chain infrastructure or PBS - Complexity (McAMM on multi-asset pools): Simple per-swap rebate accrual, no auction mechanics Rebate Accrual & Claiming: The virtuous cycle: 1. Cooperators compete to arbitrage first (rebates lower their profit threshold) 2. Competition → faster price convergence → smaller LVR window 3. High-reputation cooperators donate proceeds → LPs recover LVR losses 4. Better LP returns → more liquidity → tighter spreads 5. Tighter spreads → more arbitrage opportunities → more cooperation 6. Low-reputation cooperators revoked → only aligned actors remain We call these participants "Cooperators" or "Cooperative Arbitrageurs"—transforming adversarial extraction into collaborative market-making. See: Manifesto - Cooperative Arbitrage 4. Comparison with Other AMMs 4.1. Uniswap V2/V3 Uniswap: - Static fees (0.05%, 0.3%, 1%) - No volatility adaptation - No inventory awareness - JIT vulnerable (V3 concentrated liquidity) AIMM Advantage: - Dynamic fees respond to risk - Inventory skew protection - Dual TWAP manipulation resistance 4.2. Balancer V2 Balancer: - Static fees per pool - Oracle price feeds (external dependency) - No built-in JIT protection AIMM Advantage: - Market-aware bi-factor dynamic fees - Internal + external oracle redundancy - Volatility-aware pricing 4.3. Curve V2 (LLAMMA) Curve: - Dynamic fees via internal oracle - Inventory-based repricing - No explicit volatility component AIMM Advantage: - Explicit volatility measurement and fees - Dual-window TWAP (more manipulation resistant) - Configurable sensitivity parameters 4.4. State-of-the-Art LVR Mitigation Comparison AIMM's Cooperative Arbitrage fits within the landscape of LVR mitigation research as a rebate-style, whitelisted revenue redistribution mechanism that avoids the strong oracle and block-builder assumptions of competing designs. 4.4.1. McAMM (MEV-Capturing AMM) What it is: McAMM auctions the right to be the first trader in each block. Arbitrageurs bid for this slot, and the winning bid goes to LPs, internalizing MEV that would otherwise be extracted.[^1][^2] How it fights LVR: When external price moves, the first-trade slot captures most arbitrage value. By auctioning it, LPs recapture what they'd lose to informed flow.[^2][^4] Pros: - Conceptually clean - Minimal AMM changes - Strongly LVR-reducing with competitive auctions Cons: - Block-builder dependent: Requires PBS (proposer-builder separation) and builders who respect the auction—only realistic on Ethereum mainnet with MEV-boost[^1][^4] - Anti-democratizing: Professional MEV shops integrated with builders dominate; retail arbitrage priced out - Portability issues: Thin auctions on chains without mature MEV infrastructure - Multi-asset complexity: "First trade of block" must translate to "first batch" across N tokens, complicating auction and MEV search Why AIMM chose differently: Cross-chain deployment requires solutions that work without builder infrastructure. McAMM is Ethereum-specific. 4.4.2. am-AMM (Auction-Managed AMM) What it is: Harberger-style auction for a pool manager lease. Winner pays continuous rent to LPs and in return controls fee schedules and captures all internal arbitrage profits.[^7][^8][^9] How it fights LVR: Manager continuously arbs the pool vs. external markets, internalizing MEV while paying competitive rent upfront. LPs recover LVR via rent payments and optimized fees.[^5][^7] Pros: - Economically elegant - Unifies LVR reduction and fee optimization - Chain-agnostic (only needs on-chain auction) Cons: - Centralizing: Single large manager controls all fees and trading revenue at any time[^7][^9] - Manager trust: Malicious or absent manager creates governance risk - Oracle dependency in practice: Competitive managers need off-chain CEX feeds and HFT infrastructure - Anti-democratizing: Smaller players locked out until they can outbid incumbent Why AIMM chose differently: Manager trust and centralization conflict with AIMM's permissionless design goals. We prefer distributed competition among multiple cooperators rather than winner-take-all auctions. 4.4.3. UAMM (Oracle-Driven AMM) What it is: AMM that derives price from external oracles rather than pool balances, adding slippage only to manage inventory toward a target.[^11][^12] How it fights LVR: If oracles reflect true market price, UAMM quotes near-oracle prices, leaving essentially no arbitrage gap. Classical LVR from stale prices disappears.[^10][^11] Pros: - Strongest LVR solution theoretically (if oracle is perfect) - Eliminates arbitrage opportunities at the source Cons: - Oracle-centric and fragile: Wrong, manipulated, or lagging oracle → unbounded LP losses[^10][^11] - Single point of failure: AMM safety = oracle safety - Centralization: Oracle choice, update frequency, and failover are governance decisions - Lag still exists: Even fast oracles (Pyth, Chainlink) lag CEX prices by seconds; LVR reduced but not eliminated Related designs: DODO, Swaap, and other oracle-first AMMs share these tradeoffs. Why AIMM chose differently: Oracle-first designs trade decentralization for LVR reduction. AIMM's internal TWAP + optional external fallback provides redundancy without single-point dependency. 4.4.4. AIMM's Cooperative Arbitrage What it is: Whitelisted arbitrageurs earn rebates proportional to their reputation (donations/rebates ratio), incentivizing them to donate arbitrage proceeds back to the pool. How it fights LVR: - Rebates lower cooperators' profit threshold → they arbitrage faster → smaller LVR window - High-reputation cooperators donate proceeds → LPs recover LVR losses directly - DAO can run its own bot with 100% donation rate → maximal reputation → closes LVR loop entirely Comparison: | Approach | Portability | Centralization | Oracle Dependency | LVR Reduction | Permissionless? | |----------|-------------|----------------|-------------------|---------------|-----------------| | McAMM | Low (PBS only) | Medium (pro MEV shops) | None | High | Yes (auction open) | | am-AMM | High | High (single manager) | Practical (manager needs CEX) | Very High | Yes (auction open) | | UAMM | High | Very High (oracle control) | Total | Highest (if oracle perfect) | Yes (trading open) | | AIMM Coop Arb | High | Medium (DAO whitelist) | None (internal TWAP) | High (via donations) | No (whitelist) | Key differentiators: 1. No builder dependency: Works on any EVM chain, not just Ethereum with PBS 2. Distributed competition: Multiple cooperators (max 10) instead of single manager 3. No oracle single-point-of-failure: Internal TWAP with optional external fallback 4. Simple per-swap mechanics: No auctions, no manager leases—just rebate accrual 5. Emergent DAO advantage: Any cooperator can compete, but 100% donation rate naturally dominates Tradeoff: Not fully permissionless (requires DAO curation), but avoids strong trust assumptions of oracle-first or manager-controlled designs. Why this works: AIMM's dynamic fee model already prices LVR risk via volatility and inventory components. Cooperative Arbitrage adds a revenue redistribution layer that returns extracted value to LPs without requiring perfect oracles or centralized managers. [^1]: https://ethresear.ch/t/mev-capturing-amm-mcamm/13336 [^2]: https://www.gate.com/learn/articles/-introduction-to-mev-mitigation/5121 [^4]: https://www.pyth.network/blog/beyond-the-dark-forest-experiments-in-mitigating-mev [^5]: https://anthonyleezhang.github.io/pdfs/lvr.pdf [^7]: https://arxiv.org/html/2403.03367v1 [^8]: https://fc25.ifca.ai/preproceedings/183.pdf [^9]: https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.03367 [^10]: https://fenbushi.vc/2024/01/20/ending-lps-losing-game-exploring-the-loss-versus-rebalancing-lvr-problem-and-its-solutions/ [^11]: https://arxiv.org/html/2308.06375v2 [^12]: https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.06375 5. Configuration 5.1. Asset-Level Parameters 5.2. Recommended Ranges | Asset Class | gamma | vega | lambda | minFee | maxFee | |-------------|-------|------|--------|--------|--------| | Stablecoins | 5000-10000 | 5000-8000 | 8000-12000 | 1-3 bps | 50-100 bps | | Major pairs | 10000-15000 | 10000-15000 | 10000-15000 | 5-10 bps | 100-300 bps | | Volatile alts | 15000-25000 | 15000-25000 | 15000-25000 | 10-30 bps | 300-1000 bps | 5.3. Tuning Guidelines Conservative (maximize LP protection): - Higher vega → stronger volatility penalties - Higher lambda → stronger inventory penalties - Higher minFee → baseline protection Aggressive (maximize volume): - Lower sensitivity parameters - Lower minFee - Rely on haircuts for extreme events Balanced (default): - Moderate parameters (10000 = 1.0× multiplier) - Caps at maxFee for tail events - Tested against historical data 6. Monitoring & Alerts On-Chain Metrics: - Real-time coverage ratios - Fee tier distribution - Swap directionality (buy/sell pressure) - Volatility EMAs Off-Chain Analytics**: - LP vs arbitrageur PnL segregation - Adverse selection cost estimation - CEX-DEX price correlation - JIT detection (when implemented) 7. Related Documentation - Inventory Management - Coverage and skew formulas - Spread & Fees - Complete fee model - Internal Oracle - TWAP implementation - Security Overview - Broader security model

documents.title: 1.1.3. Anchor Path Pricing
documents.content: Anchor Path Pricing Assets priced through anchor paths (lowest common ancestor routing) while accounted in base denomination (O(N) complexity, natural asset relationships) Problem: Hub-and-Spoke Limitations Issue 1: Volatility Misrepresentation - Trading correlated assets (wstETH→WETH) used √(σWETH/USDC × σwstETH/USDC) ≈ 49% - Actual correlation only ~2% volatility Issue 2: Liquidity Profile Mismatch - Assets priced against USDC even when naturally trading against other assets - wstETH liquidity should concentrate against WETH, not USDC Core Innovation: Tree-Based Routing Assets form a tree where: - Root: Base token (USDC, no anchor) - Each asset: Has one anchor (parent node) defining pricing relationship - Swaps route: Through anchor paths via lowest common ancestor (LCA) Result: O(N) complexity + economically accurate pricing Graph Topology Constraints: - Maximum depth: 4 (root at 0, leaves at ≤4) - Single root guarantees acyclicity - Each asset: exactly one anchor - Every asset: path to root Anchor Path Examples | Route | Path | LCA | Hops | |-------|------|-----|------| | USDT→DAI | USDT → USDC → DAI | USDC | 2 | | wstETH→WETH | wstETH → WETH | WETH | 1 | | wstETH→rETH | wstETH → WETH → rETH | WETH | 2 | | USDT→wstETH | USDT → USDC → WETH → wstETH | USDC | 3 | Max path: 2×depth = 8 hops for depth-4 tree (capped at 6) Hop Semantics Each hop has distinct behavior based on position in anchor path: | Hop Type | Reserves | Pricing | Oracle | Purpose | |----------|----------|---------|--------|---------| | Edge (1st/last) | ✓ Change | Full impact | Required | Consume liquidity | | Intermediate (middle) | ✗ Fixed | Mid-price only | Price only | Numeraire transform | Example (USDT→wstETH via USDC→WETH): 1. USDT→USDC (edge): Price impact on both, reserve changes 2. USDC→WETH (intermediate): Mid-price only, no reserve change 3. WETH→wstETH (edge): Price impact on both, reserve changes Risk Aggregation Per-Hop Signals Volatility (blend recent + baseline): Deviation (multi-timeframe disagreement): Path-Level Risk Conservative max across all hops: Rationale: Path risk dominated by noisiest hop. If WETH (intermediate node) moves 10% during swap, trader bears that risk. Spread Calculation Only endpoint parameters (where reserves change): Volatility band (symmetric): Deviation surcharge (toxic side only): Final spread: Creates asymmetric spreads: coverage-improving trades pay volatility band (arb-friendly), coverage-worsening trades pay extra (toxic penalty). See for full model. Key Advantages | Aspect | Hub-and-Spoke | Anchor Tree | Benefit | |--------|---------------|-------------|---------| | Correlated pair spreads | √(50% × 48%) ≈ 49% | 2% (actual) | Accurate pricing | | Oracles | N | N | O(N) scaling | | Governance | O(N) | O(N) | Simple management | | LP concentration | Suboptimal | Natural | Market-aligned | Multiple peg support: USD stablecoins (USDC anchor), ETH LSTs (WETH anchor), BTC wraps (WBTC anchor) Trade-offs | Downside | Mitigation | |----------|-----------| | Routing complexity | LCA caching, precomputed paths | | Higher gas (long paths) | Direct anchors preferred, depth limit | | Anchor concentration risk | Circuit breakers, monitoring | | Configuration complexity | Clear governance, phased rollout | Implementation Notes Oracle Requirements Each non-root asset needs oracle in terms of its anchor: - wstETH/WETH oracle - USDT/USDC oracle - WETH/USDC oracle Internal TWAP oracles preferred (no external dependencies). State Updates Only edge assets change balances: - Input asset reserves: +volume - Output asset reserves: -volume - Intermediate anchors: unchanged Migration Path 1. Phase 1: All assets→USDC (hub-and-spoke, backward compatible) 2. Phase 2: Stablecoins→USDC anchor 3. Phase 3: LSTs→WETH anchor 4. Phase 4: Wrapped assets→native anchors Security - Oracle resistance: Leaf manipulation affects only that asset; anchor manipulation affects subtree - Arbitrage: Direct wstETH/WETH arbitrage without USDC friction - Capital efficiency: LPs concentrate where naturally deep (stablecoins near parity, LSTs near staking ratio) Summary Tree-based routing elegantly balances O(N) complexity with accurate market pricing: - ✓ Correct spreads for correlated assets - ✓ Multiple simultaneous peg groups - ✓ Natural liquidity concentration - ✓ Unified risk management in base denomination Trade-offs manageable with caching, monitoring, and phased deployment.

documents.title: 1.1.5. Slippage & Price Impact
documents.content: 1.2.4.5. Slippage & Price Impact Understanding execution costs and how to protect against unexpected price deviations Overview When executing a swap, traders face two distinct types of execution costs: 1. Price Impact: The deterministic cost of trade size against available liquidity 2. Slippage: The unexpected deviation between quoted and actual execution price Understanding the difference is crucial for setting appropriate trade parameters and choosing execution strategies. Price Impact (Deterministic) Price impact is the predictable price movement caused by your trade consuming liquidity. It's known before execution and depends on: - Trade size relative to available liquidity - Liquidity depth at current price levels - AMM curve shape (invariant-based vs. spline-based) Calculation For a constant-product AMM (x·y=k): | Trade Size (% of Pool) | Approximate Impact | |-----------------------|--------------------| | 0.1% | ~0.1% | | 1% | ~1% | | 5% | ~4.8% | | 10% | ~9.1% | AIMM's Approach AIMM uses spline-based liquidity profiles rather than fixed invariant curves. This allows: - Shaped depth: Pool operators can concentrate liquidity where trading occurs most - Dynamic adjustment: Depth scales with coverage ratio and volatility - Retail-friendly: Tighter impact for small trades, wider for large The parameter controls price impact curvature: Higher volatility → wider dispersion → greater price impact protection for LPs. Slippage (Stochastic) Slippage is the unexpected difference between quoted price and execution price. Unlike price impact, slippage is unpredictable and can be positive or negative. Causes of Slippage | Source | Description | Direction | |--------|-------------|-----------| | Market movement | Price changes between quote and execution | Either | | Front-running | MEV searcher trades ahead of you | Negative | | Sandwich attacks | MEV bot manipulates price before and after | Negative | | Network latency | Delayed transaction confirmation | Either | | Oracle updates | Price feed changes during execution | Either | Positive Slippage Slippage can be positive (favorable) if the market moves in your favor between quote and execution. However, this is rare on public mempools because: 1. MEV searchers monitor pending transactions 2. Favorable price movements are captured by backrunners 3. Only unfavorable movements pass through to the original trader This asymmetry is why MEV protection matters—without it, traders experience systematically negative slippage. Protection Mechanisms 1. Parameter AIMM's function enforces slippage protection via : If execution would result in less than , the transaction reverts: Setting : - Tight tolerance (0.1-0.5%): Protects against MEV but may fail in volatile markets - Normal tolerance (0.5-1%): Balance of protection and success rate - Wide tolerance (1-3%): Higher success rate but more exposure to slippage 2. MEV-Protected RPCs Hide transactions from public mempool to prevent front-running and sandwich attacks. Free Public Endpoints (Ethereum L1) | Provider | Endpoint | Notes | |----------|----------|-------| | MEV Blocker | | CoW Protocol's protection | | Flashbots Protect | | Fast mode, may sacrifice some protection | | Merkle | | Free tier available | | Llama Nodes | | Free tier available | | BlockRazor | | MEV protection on by default | Free Public Endpoints (BNB Chain) | Provider | Endpoint | |----------|----------| | 48 Club | | | Merkle | | | Llama Nodes | | | BlockRazor | | Free Public Endpoints (Base) | Provider | Endpoint | |----------|----------| | Llama Nodes | | Private RPC Networks (Multi-Chain) | Provider | Coverage | MEV Protection | |----------|----------|----------------| | Alchemy | Ethereum, Polygon, Arbitrum, Optimism, Base | Always on | | BlockPI | Multi-chain | Enable in dashboard | | dRPC | Multi-chain | Enable in dashboard | | Helius | Solana | Optional Jito integration | 3. Timing Strategies | Strategy | Description | Trade-off | |----------|-------------|-----------| | Low volatility periods | Trade when markets are calm | May miss opportunities | | Order splitting | Break large orders into smaller pieces | Higher gas costs | | Limit orders | Set exact price (if supported) | May not execute | | Off-peak hours | Reduced MEV competition | Lower liquidity | Chain-Specific Considerations Ethereum L1 (Public Mempool) Ethereum's public mempool makes all pending transactions visible to anyone running a node. MEV searchers continuously monitor for profitable reordering opportunities. Transaction ordering: Gas auction—highest priority fee wins position in block. Protection: Use MEV-protected RPCs (listed above) to submit transactions directly to trusted block builders. Arbitrum / OP Stack Rollups (Sequencer) Transactions go directly to a centralized sequencer, which has full visibility of pending transactions but is expected to order fairly. Original ordering: FCFS (First-Come-First-Served) Current (Arbitrum): Timeboost auction for priority lane Current (Base/OP): FCFS with priority fee escalation Protection: Sequencer is trusted not to extract MEV directly. Third-party MEV is limited by sequencer control over ordering. Solana (Gulf Stream) No public mempool—transactions forwarded directly to slot leaders. The leader controls ordering. MEV infrastructure: Jito provides bundle auctions at the validator level. Protection: Helius RPC offers optional Jito integration for MEV protection. Sui (Narwhal DAG) DAG-based mempool with object-based execution model. MEV concentrated around "shared objects" (e.g., AMM pools). Ordering: Parallel execution of independent transactions reduces ordering-based MEV for simple transfers. Protection: Contention-based MEV still exists for AMM trades accessing shared pool state. Practical Recommendations For Retail Users 1. Always set to at least 99% of quoted output 2. Use MEV-protected RPCs on Ethereum and BNB Chain 3. Check gas prices—high gas often correlates with MEV activity 4. Split large trades if you're swapping more than 1% of pool depth For Integrators 1. Quote with fresh oracle prices before displaying to users 2. Calculate realistic slippage bounds based on volatility 3. Provide RPC configuration for MEV protection 4. Show price impact clearly before execution For Large Traders 1. Use intent-based systems (CoW Protocol, UniswapX) for better execution 2. Consider private mempools or direct builder connections 3. Time-weight execution across multiple blocks 4. Monitor markout to measure actual execution quality Research & Further Reading Academic Papers - Flashbots: MEV in Eth2 - MEV taxonomy and measurement - Private MEV Protection RPCs - Analysis of private RPC effectiveness - MEV on Polygon - Cross-chain MEV impact study - Cross-chain Sandwich Attacks - Multi-chain MEV vectors - High-Frequency Trading on DEXes - DEX microstructure analysis Protocol Documentation - UniswapX Price Improvement - Order flow auction design - Protected Order Flow Relay - Relay architecture - Flashbots Docs - MEV infrastructure - Jito Documentation - Solana MEV infrastructure Related Documentation - 1.1.4. documents.title: 1.1.4. Spread & Fees
documents.content: AIMM Spread & Fee Model Asymmetric spread with symmetrical fee distribution 1. Overview AIMM implements a sophisticated fee model that separates spread asymmetry (pricing) from fee distribution fairness (LP earnings): 1.1. Spread Asymmetry (Pricing) - Volatility Band $Sv$: Symmetric base spread around mid-price - Directional Surcharge $U$: Asymmetric penalty for coverage-worsening trades - Bid-Ask Spread: Different costs for coverage-improving vs coverage-worsening directions For coverage ratio definition, see Inventory Management §2. 1.2. Fee Distribution Symmetry (LP Fairness) - 50/50 Split: Half of fee taken from input token, half from output token - Fair LP Earnings: LPs earn fees in both tokens regardless of trade direction - No One-Sided Fee Problem: Unlike traditional AMMs where fees concentrate in one token 2. Unit System 2.1. BPS Precision All fees and spreads use 0.0001% precision (not standard 0.01% bps): $$B = 1,000,000$$ where $B$ = BPSPRECISION. This means: - 1 unit = 0.0001% - 10,000 units = 1% - 100 units = 0.01% (1 standard bps) 2.2. Fee Bounds | Parameter | Type | Max Value | Max Fee | |-----------|------|-----------|---------| | | uint16 | 65,535 | ~6.5% | | | uint16 | 65,535 | ~6.5% | 2.3. Volatility Units Volatility $sigma$ uses 1e6 base: - 1,000,000 = 1% - 10,000,000 = 10% 3. Spread Calculation 3.1. Risk Signals Volatility and deviation are used here as pricing risk signals. For how these values are computed and updated, see Internal Oracle §8-11. Per-Hop Volatility $sigma$: $$\sigmai = \frac{\sigma{f,i} + \sigma{s,i}}{2}$$ where: - σf = fast EMA volatility - σs = slow EMA volatility Per-Hop Deviation: $$\Deltai = \max(|o{f,i} - o{s,i}|, |o{f,i}|)$$ where: - o{f,i} = fast TWAP offset at hop i - o{s,i} = slow TWAP offset at hop i Path-Level Aggregation: $$\sigmap = \maxi(\sigmai)$$ $$\Deltap = \maxi(\Deltai)$$ 3.2. Symmetric Volatility Band Baseline spread, direction-agnostic: $$Sv = 100 + \frac{\sigmap \times \nu}{100 \times M}$$ where: - Sv = volatility band (basis points) - σp = path volatility - ν = max(νin, νout) (vega, endpoint-only) - M = MULTBASE (10000) - Units: 0.0001% precision (B = 1,000,000) 3.3. Directional Deviation Surcharge Asymmetric penalty for informed/toxic flow: $$U = \frac{\Deltap \times \lambda}{M}$$ where: - U = deviation surcharge - Δp = path deviation - λ = max(λin, λout) (lambda, endpoint-only) - M = MULTBASE (10000) 3.4. Coverage Classification $$c = \frac{R}{L}$$ $$I0 = |c{\text{in},0} - 1| + |c{\text{out},0} - 1|$$ $$I1 = |c{\text{in},1} - 1| + |c{\text{out},1} - 1|$$ $$\text{improves} = (I1 1$): - Buying from pool (reduces reserves) → improves coverage → pays $Sv$ only - Selling to pool (increases reserves) → worsens coverage → pays $Sv + U$ When pool is under-collateralized ($c < 1$): - Buying from pool → worsens coverage → pays $Sv + U$ - Selling to pool → improves coverage → pays $Sv$ only At equilibrium ($c ~~ 1$): - Both directions pay similar spreads unless deviation high 5.3. Economic Interpretation Volatility Band $Sv$: Market maker spread covering: - Expected adverse selection - Inventory rebalancing costs - Option value of providing liquidity Deviation Surcharge $U$: Informed flow penalty: - High $Delta$ signals oracle disagreement - Coverage-worsening trades during uncertainty pay extra - Prevents exploitation during price manipulation 6. Protocol Fee Split 6.1. Revenue Sharing After calculating total fees (50% from input + 50% from output): $$\phi{\text{proto}} = \phi \times \frac{r}{100}$$ $$\phi{\text{lp}} = \phi - \phi{\text{proto}}$$ where: - φproto = protocol fee portion - φlp = LP fee portion - φ = total fees - r = protocol share percentage (0-100) 6.2. Proto Share Parameter | Proto Share | Type | Distribution | |-------------|------|--------------| | 0 | uint8 | 100% to LPs | | 25 | uint8 | 25% protocol, 75% LPs (default) | | 50 | uint8 | 50/50 split | is a uint8 with base 100 (0-100 range representing 0%-100%). 7. Fee Bounds 7.1. Per-Asset Configuration Each asset defines fee-related parameters: - , : Floor/ceiling in 0.0001% units - : Volatility sensitivity (basis 10000) - : Deviation sensitivity (basis 10000) See: Parametrization 7.2. Path-Level Bounds For multi-hop swaps: $$f{\min,p} = \maxi(f{\min,i})$$ $$f{\max,p} = \maxi(f{\max,i})$$ $$S = \text{clamp}(S{\text{raw}}, f{\min,p}, f{\max,p})$$ where: - fmin,p = path-level minimum fee - fmax,p = path-level maximum fee - Sraw = unclamped spread - i = index over all hops in path 8. Comparison with Other AMMs 8.1. Fee Token Location | Protocol | Fee Taken In | Distribution | |----------|--------------|--------------| | Uniswap V2/V3 | 100% input | One-sided LP earnings | | Trader Joe V2 | 100% input | One-sided LP earnings | | Curve V1 | 100% output | One-sided LP earnings | | Wombat | Input, redistributed | Single-asset LP friendly | | AIMM | 50% input + 50% output | Symmetrical LP earnings | 8.2. Spread Characteristics | Aspect | Uniswap V3 | AIMM | |--------|------------|------| | Fee structure | Fixed tiers (0.01-1%) | Market-aware (bi-factor) | | Volatility response | None | σ-scaled band | | Inventory response | None | Skew + surcharge | | Coverage awareness | No | Yes (directional) | | LVR mitigation | Via hooks only | Built-in surcharge | | Fee distribution | One-sided (input) | Symmetrical (50/50) | 9. Parameter Guidelines 9.1. Vega (Volatility Sensitivity) - Basis: 10,000 = 1.0x sensitivity - Example: $nu = 10000$, $sigma = 1,000,000$ (1%) → $Sv ~~ 200$ units (0.02%) - Tuning: Higher vega → wider spreads for volatile assets 9.2. Lambda (Deviation Sensitivity) - Basis: 10,000 = 1.0x sensitivity - Example: $lambda = 10000$, $Delta = 500,000$ → $U ~~ 50$ units (0.005%) - Tuning: Higher lambda → larger penalty during oracle disagreement 9.3. Fee Bounds - Units: 0.0001% precision ($B = 1,000,000$) - Example: $f("min") = 100$ (0.01%), $f("max") = 50000$ (5%) - Purpose: Prevent extreme spreads (max) and free-option attacks (min) 10. Multi-Hop Fee Aggregation 10.1. Path Structure For swap A → B through intermediate hops: 10.2. Signal Aggregation | Signal | Aggregation | Rationale | |--------|-------------|-----------| | $sigmap$ | $max(sigmai)$ across legs | Conservative uncertainty | | $Deltap$ | $max(Deltai)$ across legs | Conservative deviation | | $nu$ | $max$ (endpoints only) | Risk at edges | | $lambda$ | $max$ (endpoints only) | Risk at edges | | $f("min")$ | $max$ (all legs) | Strictest floor | | $f("max")$ | $max$ (all legs) | Strictest ceiling | 10.3. Edge vs Intermediate Pricing - Edge hops (first/last): Full price impact via spline traversal - Intermediate hops: Mid-price only (no impact accumulation) 11. Implementation Reference Key functions in : - : Spread calculation with caching - : Protocol/LP fee division 12. Economic Benefits 12.1. For Liquidity Providers Symmetrical Fee Earnings: - Earn fees in both tokens proportionally - No concentration risk from one-sided fees - Better portfolio balance maintenance Coverage Protection: - Fees retained in reserves improve coverage - Higher coverage → better LP protection - Lower withdrawal haircuts 12.2. For Traders Fair Pricing: - Spread reflects actual market conditions (volatility + deviation) - Coverage-improving trades get better prices (arb-friendly) - Coverage-worsening trades pay fair premium during uncertainty Predictable Costs: - Bounded fees prevent extreme spreads - Transparent market-aware model - No hidden LVR extraction 13. Flash Loan Fees 13.1. Base Fee Fixed percentage of borrowed amount: $$phi("flash") = (x f("flash")) / B$$ where $f("flash")$ = flash fee in bps. 13.2. Parameters | Parameter | Type | Default | Description | |-----------|------|---------|-------------| | | uint16 | 90 | 0.009% flash loan fee | 14. Related Documentation - Inventory Management — Coverage impact calculation - Internal Oracle — σ and Δ computation - Liquidity Shaping — Spline-based depth - Toxic Flow Mitigation — Protection mechanisms - Parametrization — Complete parameter reference 15. References - Empirical spread-volatility linearity: Relation between Bid-Ask Spread, Impact and Volatility - Multi-timeframe uncertainty: Volatility, Information Feedback and Market Microstructure Noise - Inventory-aware pricing: Inventory Risk and Market Making

documents.title: Overview
documents.content: AIMM System Architecture Technical overview of the Adaptive Inventory Market Maker protocol 1. Overview AIMM is a multi-asset AMM designed for passive liquidity providers. Core components: - Single-sided deposits — LPs deposit one token, receive fungible LP tokens - N-asset pooling — Anchor tree topology enables any-to-any routing - Inventory-based pricing — Avellaneda-Stoikov inspired mid-price adjustment - Coverage-aware ALM — Reserves/liabilities separation (Wombat-style) - Catmull-Rom spline profiles — Algo-optimized, depth curves supporting non-uniform and multimodal distributions - Internal TWAP oracle — Multi-timeframe (eg. 5min/1hr) with support for external fallback - Diamond-lite proxy — Modular module upgrades via ERC-7201 namespaced storage 2. Contract Architecture 2.1. Diamond-Lite Proxy (PoolProxyV1) All pool interactions route through a single proxy that dispatches to implementation modules via : Storage Isolation: Each module uses ERC-7201 namespaced storage to prevent collisions. 2.2. Core Modules | Module | Purpose | Key Functions | |--------|---------|---------------| | CoreV1 | Main AMM operations | , , , , | | InternalOracleV1 | TWAP tracking | Auto-updated on swaps, dual-window EMAs | | AdminV1 | Configuration | Asset management, fee params, timelocks | | FlashV1 | Flash loans | ERC-3156 compliant | | StakingV1 | Governance staking | LP + gov token staking, voting power | | DistributorV1 | Rewards | Accumulator-based distribution | | RescueV1 | Emergency | Token rescue, admin recovery | 3. Core Data Structures Per-asset state includes reserves, liabilities, pricing parameters, and sensitivity coefficients. See for struct definitions. Key per-asset fields: - Reserves & liabilities for coverage tracking - Anchor pointer for tree routing - Sensitivity params: gamma, vega, lambda - Fee bounds: minFeeBps, maxFeeBps See: Parametrization for full field reference. 4. Pricing System 4.1. Pipeline 4.2. Key Concepts - Coverage Ratio: — measures asset health - Inventory Skew: Linear Avellaneda-Stoikov adjustment (±100 range) - Spread: Volatility-based fee with toxic flow surcharge - Spline Traversal: Price impact via liquidity profile integration See: - Inventory Management — Coverage, skew, withdrawal haircuts - Spread & Fees — Fee calculation - Liquidity Shaping — Spline profiles 5. Anchor Tree Routing All tokens connect through an anchor tree with a hub token (typically stablecoin) as root. 5.1. Topology 5.2. Swap Routing (LCA Algorithm) Swaps path through the Least Common Ancestor: Route: Hops: Constraints: - Max depth: 4 - Max path length: 6 hops (2 × MAXDEPTH) - No cycles allowed See: Anchor Path Pricing 6. Oracle System 6.1. Internal Oracle Auto-updated on every swap with: - Dual TWAP windows: Fast (5min) + Slow (1hr) - Dual volatility EMAs: Responsive + Stable - B64 encoding: Compact 64-bit price storage See: Internal Oracle for full details. 6.2. Gas Optimization Oracle reads are cached in transient storage (EIP-1153): - First read: ~2,100 gas (external call) - Subsequent reads: ~100 gas (transient load) 7. Coverage-Aware ALM Asset-Liability Management (ALM) tracks reserves vs LP claims per asset: - Coverage Ratio: (100% = equilibrium) - Undercollateralized ( ): Withdrawal haircuts apply - Overcollateralized ( ): Surplus available Safety Mechanisms: - Withdrawal haircuts protect remaining LPs when - Liability decay gradually restores coverage in emergencies See: Inventory Management for formulas and details. 8. Liquidity Profiles Catmull-Rom spline profiles define liquidity distribution across the depth curve: - 1-16 weight segments with monotone cubic interpolation - Exact analytical integration for price impact calculation - Customizable shapes: Concentrated, uniform, multimodal See: Liquidity Shaping for profile design and examples. 9. Storage Layout (ERC-7201) 9.1. Namespaced Slots | Module | Location | Purpose | |--------|----------|---------| | Core | | Assets, balances, config | | Oracle | | Feed accumulators | | Staking | | Stakes, voting power | | Distributor | | Campaigns, rewards | 9.2. Transient Storage (EIP-1153) Used for: - Reentrancy guards - Oracle price caching (~2,100 gas/hit saved) - Flash loan state 10. Governance & Timelocks 10.1. Operation Types | OpType | Delay | Risk Level | |--------|-------|------------| | TRANSFEROWNERSHIP | 3 days | HIGH | | UPDATEMODULE | 2 days | BASE | | MIGRATEBASETOKEN | 7 days | CRITICAL | | UPDATEORACLE | 2 days | BASE | | ADDASSET | 1 day | LOW | | UPDATEFEES | 1 day | LOW | 10.2. Two-Phase Execution 1. → stores pending 2. Wait for delay 3. → applies within grace period 11. Key Invariants 11.1. Coverage Bounds - → equilibrium - → undercollateralized (haircuts apply) - → overcollateralized 11.2. Skew Bounds 11.3. Fee Bounds Where fees use 0.0001% precision (BPS_PRECISION = 1,000,000). 11.4. Anchor Tree 12. Gas Optimizations | Optimization | Savings | |--------------|---------| | Single-slot FeedData packing | ~2,100 gas/read | | B64 encoding | 75% storage reduction | | Transient oracle caching | ~2,100 gas/hit | | Packed timelocks | 66% slot reduction | | LCA without path caching | Storage-free routing | | Bitmask hooks | 32 bits vs N mappings | 13. Error Handling Minimal consolidated error set: | Error | Usage | |-------|-------| | | Zero address/amount/price | | | Balance checks | | | Limit exceeded | | | Not initialized/paused | | | Swap/flash disabled | | | Missing config | | | Slippage/coverage | | | Oracle staleness | | | Guard triggered | See: 14. Contract Deployment 14.1. Immutable Components - Library contracts (LibPricing, LibOracle, LibSpline, LibMaths) - Factory contracts 14.2. Upgradeable via Proxy - PoolProxyV1 (dispatcher) - All modules (CoreV1, AdminV1, etc.) 14.3. Upgradeable via UUPS - TreasuryV1 - BridgeV1 15. Related Documentation - Inventory Management — Pricing mechanics - Core Module — Module documentation - Parametrization — Parameter reference

documents.title: 1.3.4. Bridging
documents.content: Cross-Chain Bridging 1. Overview The protocol implements cross-chain bridging for BTR governance tokens (staked and unstaked) and eligible LP tokens using the ERC-7802 standard. Despite using LayerZero V2 in its current state, the bridge is designed to be messaging-protocol agnostic to support alternatives on upgrade (eg. Chainlink CCIP, Axelar GMP...). 2. Architecture 2.1. Components 1. Bridge Contract ( ) - Standalone contract (not a pool module) - Implements LayerZero V2 OApp pattern - Manages token burn/mint on source/destination - Enforces daily rate limits per token 2. ERC-7802 Tokens - BTR, sBTR, and LP tokens implement - Provides and functions - Bridge has minter/burner roles 3. LayerZero Integration - Uses LayerZero V2 endpoint - Peer-to-peer bridge configuration - Native gas payment for cross-chain messages 3. Technical Details 3.1. Bridge Flow 3.1.1. Outbound (Source Chain) 1. Initiate Bridge 2. Limit Check - Check daily outbound limit (B64-encoded) - Verify token is supported and not paused - Reset counters if new day 3. Burn Tokens 4. Send Message - Encode: - Send via LayerZero with exact native fee - Emit event with nonce 3.1.2. Inbound (Destination Chain) 1. Receive Message - LayerZero calls - Verify sender is trusted peer 2. Limit Check - Check daily inbound limit (percentage of outbound limit) - Reset counters if new day 3. Mint Tokens 4. Emit Event - Log bridging with direction flag 3.2. Rate Limiting The bridge uses B64 float encoding for gas-efficient daily limits: Daily Limits: - Outbound: Absolute limit per token - Inbound: Percentage of outbound (e.g., 120% = ) - Reset: Automatically at UTC midnight Special Cases: - flag: No limits enforced - Missing config: Reverts with 3.3. Fee Quoting NB: Transaction reverts if (exact payment required). 4. Configuration 4.1. Token Setup Initial configuration (no timelock): 4.2. Updating Configuration Changes require 2-day timelock: 4.3. Peer Configuration Setting LayerZero peers requires 2-day timelock: 5. Emergency Controls 5.1. Token Pause (Instant) Bridge owner can instantly pause bridging for a token: Effect: Prevents both inbound and outbound bridging immediately. 5.2. Cancel Pending Operations 6. Governance & Access Control 6.1. Bridge Owner - Initial: DAO Council multisig (3-of-5 at launch) - Long-term: Elected DAO council - Powers: - Configure token bridging parameters - Set LayerZero peer addresses - Pause/unpause tokens (emergency) - Rescue stuck tokens - Migrate to new bridge infrastructure 6.2. Timelocks | Operation | Delay | Bypass | |-----------|-------|--------| | Token config change | 2 days | No | | Set peer address | 2 days | No | | Pause token | None | N/A | | Unpause token | None | N/A | | Rescue tokens | None | No | Grace Period: 3 days after timelock expires 7. Security Features 7.1. Trusted Peers - Each chain has exactly one trusted peer bridge - Inbound messages verified against - Prevents unauthorized minting 7.2. Rate Limits - Daily limits prevent catastrophic loss - Separate inbound/outbound tracking - B64 encoding prevents manipulation - Automatic daily reset 7.3. Reentrancy Protection - All external functions use - Prevents callback exploits 7.4. Balance Verification - Outbound: Burn before send - Inbound: Verify peer before mint - No intermediate custody 8. Monitoring 8.1. Events 8.2. Queries 9. Integration Examples 9.1. Basic Bridging 9.2. Custom LayerZero Options 10. Supported Chains (Launch) | Chain | Endpoint ID | Status | |-------|-------------|--------| | Ethereum | 101 | Planned | | Arbitrum | 110 | Planned | | Optimism | 111 | Planned | | Base | 184 | Planned | NB: Actual deployment depends on DAO governance decisions. 11. Bridgeable Assets At launch, the following assets are bridgeable: 1. BTR: Unstaked governance token 2. sBTR: Staked governance token 3. LP Tokens: Marked with in risk config Pool curators can enable bridging for their LP tokens via: 12. Migration Strategy The bridge architecture supports migration to alternative bridges: 12.1. Adding New Bridge 1. Deploy new bridge contract 2. Grant mint/burn permissions to new bridge 3. Configure rate limits 4. Announce migration timeline 5. Disable old bridge after grace period 12.2. Supported Bridge Standards - LayerZero V2 (current) The bridge is designed to be messaging-protocol agnostic. Alternative providers (CCIP, Axelar, Hyperlane) can be added via timelocked operations if needed. 13. Best Practices 13.1. For Users - Always quote fees before bridging - Use sufficient gas limits for complex operations - Verify destination address format (bytes32) - Check daily limits before large transfers - Monitor LayerZero message status 13.2. For Integrators - Handle LayerZero delivery failures - Implement retry logic for failed messages - Cache fee quotes (valid for ~5 minutes) - Support manual message execution via LayerZero scan - Display estimated delivery time (5-30 minutes) 13.3. For Pool Operators - Enable bridging only for liquid LP tokens - Set conservative daily limits initially - Monitor bridge activity via events - Coordinate with bridge owner for config changes 14. Error Handling | Error | Cause | Solution | |-------|-------|----------| | | Token not configured | Add via | | | Token paused | Wait for unpause | | | Over daily limit | Wait for daily reset or request limit increase | | | Wrong msg.value | Use quoted fee exactly | | | Destination chain not set | Configure peer via | | | Message from untrusted peer | Contact DAO council |

documents.title: 1.3.1. Composability
documents.content: Composability Standard interfaces and integration patterns for external protocols to interact with AIMM pools 1. Overview Composability enables external protocols, applications, and users to seamlessly integrate with AIMM pools through standardized interfaces. Rather than forking code or maintaining custom adaptations, external developers use: - Public pool interfaces: Standardized function signatures for swaps, liquidity provision, staking - ERC standards: ERC-20 (tokens), ERC-3156 (flash loans), ERC-7201 (storage layout) - Modular architecture: Swap any combination of tokens, query prices, execute flash loans - SDK integration: TypeScript utilities for quote calculation, transaction building, reward tracking Key principle: AIMM prioritizes open interfaces over walled-garden integrations. 2. Core Integration Patterns 2.1. Token Swaps Interface: (module selector ) Function: Integration flow: 1. Quote calculation: - Call (read-only) - Returns spread, fees, oracle prices, skew impact - Calculate 2. Token approval: - If swapping non-native token: - If swapping native (ETH): Send via 3. Execute swap: - Call with recipient address - Pool route: Swap module → Oracle update → Fee distribution - Emits: 4. Slippage protection: - Revert if - Typical slippage: 0.1% - 1% depending on swap size SDK helper ( ): Common use cases: - DEX aggregators (1inch, 0x) routing through AIMM - Liquidation bots swapping collateral for repayment assets - Rebalancing protocols maintaining portfolio ratios - Bridge contracts (LayerZero) swapping received assets 2.2. Liquidity Provision Interface: (module selector ) Functions: Deposit: Withdrawal: Integration flow: 1. Approve LP token (if withdrawing): - Not needed for deposit (tokens only) - For withdrawal: 2. Deposit flow: - Check coverage ratio before deposit (ALM constraint) - Approve token: - Call - Receive LP tokens for deposited assets - Can immediately stake LP tokens for emissions 3. Withdrawal flow: - Check if LP tokens exist: - Call - Receive underlying asset (may include haircut if coverage $100k): 0.5% - 2%+ 5.2. Flash Loan Safety Always verify flash loan callback: 5.3. Staking Cooldowns Respect 2-week LP unstaking delay: Don't assume immediate liquidity. 5.4. Voting Power Snapshots Voting power is frozen at snapshot block: Flash loans won't work for voting attacks due to snapshot finality. 6. Code References 6.1. Core Pool Interface File: Key structs: - — Inventory, liabilities, pricing parameters - — Quote output with fees and impact - / — Transaction outcomes - — Per-asset risk parameters 6.2. Staking Interface File: Functions: - — Stake BTR - — Stake LP - / — Initiate unstake - — Delegate voting power 6.3. Flash Loan Interface File: ERC-3156 compliant: - - - 6.4. SDK Location: Key modules: - — Swap execution - — Liquidity provision - — Flash loan receiver - — Voting power calculation - — Price feed integration 7. Related Documentation - Architecture Overview — Pool structure and module design - Swap & Fees — Fee mechanics - Emissions Control — Reward distribution - Liquid Staking — Staking mechanics References - ERC-3156: Flash Loans Standard - ERC-20: Token Standard - ERC-7201: Namespaced Storage Layout

documents.title: 1.3.3. Curation & White Labelling
documents.content: Curation & White Labelling Custom pool deployment, token curation, and white-label integration for protocols and operators 1. Overview Pool curation in AIMM enables any protocol, exchange, or operator to: - Deploy custom pools with their own token lists, pricing curves, and risk parameters - Manage pool ownership via timelock governance (protect against rash decisions) - Add/remove tokens dynamically using an asset request + execute pattern - Extend functionality by deploying custom hook contracts for specialized logic - Implement modules as diamond-pattern facets for unlimited extensibility - White-label the entire pool proxy as their own branded interface Key principle: AIMM is fully permissionless — anyone can deploy, no central approval needed. We welcome interested teams to reach out for strategic partnerships. 2. Pool Ownership & Control 2.1. Pool Deployment Any address can deploy a new instance: Access control: - Deployer: Can only initialize once - Owner: Controls all administrative functions (add assets, set hooks, freeze assets) - Timelock: Protects major changes (1-7 day delays) - Users: Can deposit, withdraw, swap freely (subject to pool settings) 2.2. Ownership Model | Action | Authority | Timelock | Notes | |--------|-----------|----------|-------| | Freeze/unfreeze asset | Owner | None | Emergency powers, immediate effect | | Set pricing anchor | Owner | None | Adjust pricing tree topology | | Set flow cooldown | Owner | None | Configure JIT protection (0-256 sec) | | Add asset | Owner | 1 day | Request → wait → execute pattern | | Update risk config | Owner | 1 day | Change per-asset risk parameters | | Register module | Owner | 3 days | Add new functionality (swap, flash, etc.) | | Transfer ownership | Owner | 3 days | Handoff to new operator | | Migrate base token | Owner | 7 days | Change anchor (critical, rarely done) | 3. Token Curation 3.1. Adding Tokens (Asset Manager Pattern) Two-phase process (prevents configuration mistakes): Phase 1: Request asset addition Phase 2: Execute after 1-day timelock 3.2. Oracle Configuration Three oracle modes: | Mode | Primary | Secondary | Use Case | |------|---------|-----------|----------| | Internal | Pool's TWAP | None | Stablecoins (USDC, USDT), most tokens | | External | Chainlink/Pyth | Pool TWAP fallback | Exotic assets, price feeds unavailable internally | | Hybrid | Fallback chain | Pool TWAP | Maximum safety for critical assets | Configuration struct: Precision selection ( ): - 6 decimals: Stablecoins (USDC, USDT, USDS) - price change: $0.000001 - 8 decimals: Natural assets (LINK, UNI) - price change: $0.00000001 - 12 decimals: ETH/major assets - price change: $0.000000000001 - 18 decimals: Exotics with extreme volatility - maximum precision 3.3. Risk Configuration Coverage-based logic: - 100%+ coverage: No penalties, optimal pricing - 98-100%: Decay activates, withdrawal haircuts begin (encourages rebalancing) - 50% floor: Critical; swaps may be disabled if breached Flags: See Parametrization §3.1 for complete flag reference. Common flags: (0x0002), (0x0010), (0x0001). 3.4. Liquidity Profile (Distribution Curve) Segment-based distribution for customizable price impact: Impact on pricing: - Concentrated profiles: Lower slippage near mid-price, higher on extremes - Uniform profiles: Consistent slippage across range - Custom profiles: Tailor to expected trading patterns (stablecoin vs. exotic) 3.5. Token Removal (Freeze vs. Deletion) Freeze token (temporary): Permanent removal: Not supported (prevents liquidity loss). Instead: - Owner should freeze the asset - Allow users to withdraw LP positions over time - Migrate to new pool if needed 4. Custom Hooks For complete hook interface and developer documentation, see Hooks System. 4.1. Curator Use Cases Hooks enable per-asset customization without modifying core pool logic: | Use Case | Hook | Example | |----------|------|---------| | Deposit bonuses | | Return to add LP bonus | | Withdrawal taxes | | Return to charge exit fee | | Dynamic fees | | Return based on volatility | | KYC/whitelist | | Revert for non-approved addresses | 4.2. Installing Hooks Hooks are called automatically on relevant events—no additional integration needed from users. 5. Custom Modules (Diamond-Lite Extensibility) 5.1. Module System Architecture AIMM uses EIP-2535 Diamond pattern lite — a lightweight function selector registry: - Each has a module registry - Fallback delegates calls to registered implementation based on selector Benefits: - Modular code (each function family in separate contract) - Upgradeable (swap implementations without redeployment) - Composable (combine features freely) - Efficient (minimal proxy overhead) 5.2. Pre-Built Modules | Module | Functions | Status | |--------|-----------|--------| | CoreV1 | , , , , | ✅ Core | | AdminV1 | Asset management, risk config, timelock | ✅ Core | | InternalOracleV1 | TWAP tracking, price feeds | ✅ Core | | FlashV1 | ERC-3156 flash loans | ✅ Core | | StakingV1 | LP/Gov token staking | ✅ Core | | DistributorV1 | Reward distribution | ✅ Core | | RescueV1 | Emergency asset recovery | ✅ Core | 5.3. Implementing Custom Modules Custom module requirements: 1. Define interface with function selectors 2. Implement using for shared state access 3. Register via with 3-day timelock Example interface (MarketMaker incentives): Registration flow: 6. White-Labelling 6.1. Pool as Branded Interface No fork required. Simply: 1. Deploy pool proxy with your configuration 2. Add your tokens (proprietary or curated list) 3. Install custom hooks for your branding (deposit bonuses, withdrawal taxes, etc.) 4. Host your own UI connecting to the pool address 5. Market as your own exchange (with BTR branding attribution) 6.2. Frontend Integration No backend complexity — all logic is on-chain and self-contained. 6.3. Branding & Attribution When white-labelling, we ask that: - Credit AIMM: Mention "Powered by AIMM" or similar in UI/docs - Link to docs: Direct interested users to official documentation - Maintain security: Don't modify pool logic (use hooks/modules instead) - Keep open: Don't create artificial barriers to token lists 6.4. Strategic Partnerships For major integrations (large exchanges, ecosystem plays), reach out to the team: - Custom oracle configurations for exotic assets - Dedicated module development (faster than DIY) - Multi-pool coordination across chains - Enhanced security audits for your instance 7. Complete Deployment Walkthrough Example: Stablecoin Exchange Deployment 8. Security Considerations 8.1. Timelock Protection All major changes are timelocked to allow users to exit if governance is compromised: - 1-day delay (low risk): Asset additions, risk config updates - 3-day delay (medium risk): Module registration, ownership transfers - 7-day delay (critical): Base token migration Example: If owner proposes adding a malicious token, users have 1 day to withdraw before it takes effect. 8.2. Access Control - Owner only: Freeze assets, add tokens, register modules - No owner transfer without notice: 3-day timelock prevents hijacking - No user impact: Users can always deposit/withdraw/swap (no owner powers here) 8.3. Hook Safety - Hooks can return arbitrary values, but cannot access other tokens (isolated execution) - Hook failures revert transactions (prevent orphaned rewards) - Owner can disable hooks anytime 9. Code References 9.1. Pool Proxy File: Functions: - — One-time setup - — Module selector routing - — ETH receiver 9.2. Asset Management File: Functions: - — Start 1-day timelock - — Finalize token addition - — Configure pricing tree - / — Emergency control 9.3. Hook Interface File: 12 lifecycle hooks covering deposits, withdrawals, swaps, donations, flash loans. 9.4. Module Examples Location: - — Swaps, deposits, withdrawals - — LP/Gov staking - — ERC-3156 flash loans 10. Related Documentation - Architecture Overview — Pool design and module system - Composability — Integration patterns - Swap & Fees — Fee mechanics - DAO Treasury — Protocol fee handling 11. Getting Started Quick checklist for deploying your custom pool: 1. Define token list: Which tokens to support? 2. Configure risk: What coverage ratios, decay rates? 3. Design hooks: Any custom deposit bonuses, fees, incentives? 4. Deploy: Use provided factory or deploy directly 5. Customize UI: Point to your pool address, theme your interface 6. Launch: Market to your users 7. (Optional) Partner: Contact team for strategic collaborations No approval required — permissionless by design.

documents.title: 1.3.2. Hooks
documents.content: Pool Hooks System Overview The Pool Hooks System provides a gas-efficient, runtime-updateable mechanism for extending pool functionality through custom logic at key lifecycle points. Hooks enable per-token customization without modifying core pool logic. Design Philosophy - Minimal: Direct inline calls, zero runtime validation overhead - Updateable: Owner can swap hook contracts without liquidity migration - Token-Centric: One hook contract per asset, finest granularity of customization - Type-Safe: ERC-165 interface detection and compile-time selector validation - Gas-Efficient: Flagged executiononly call hooks that are actually implemented Hook Interface Complete IPoolHooks Interface (12 Functions) Key Features: - 12 lifecycle hooks covering: initialization, deposits, withdrawals, swaps, donations, flash loans - Hook flags bitmask for gas optimization (specify which hooks the contract implements) - Return values enable hooks to dynamically adjust pool behavior: - / : Add/remove LP fees or incentives - : Override fees or add extra charges - : Adjust final pool reserves with signed delta Hook Semantics All hooks follow pool perspective semantics (how the pool views the operation): | Hook | Pool Action | User Action | Use Case | |------|-------------|-------------|----------| | | RECEIVES liquidity | Deposits tokens | Validate whitelist, check position limits | | | RECEIVED liquidity | Deposited tokens | Deploy to yield (Aave, Morpho), update accounting | | | GIVES liquidity back | Withdraws | Prepare withdrawal, check position state | | | GAVE liquidity back | Withdrew | Apply exit fees, rebalance reserves | | | EXCHANGES tokens | Swaps | Override fees, add extra charges | | | EXCHANGED tokens | Completed swap | Adjust reserves with delta, rebalance | | | RECEIVES donation | Donates tokens | Validate donor, check limits | | | RECEIVED donation | Completed donation | Accounting updates, redistribute yield | | | LENDS token | Borrows | Validate borrower, check risk | | | RECEIVED repayment | Repaid loan | Rebalance, update accounting | Example: User swaps USDC � BTC - Pool RECEIVES USDC (buys): + - Pool GIVES BTC (sells): + - Both tokens' hooks are called, enabling per-token custom logic Hook Storage & Registry Storage Model Architecture: - One hook contract per asset (not per-pool or per-pair) - Single contract implements all 12 hook functions and routes based on token parameter - Hook flags enable gas optimization: unset flags = hook not called Hook Flags Constants Usage Pattern: Hook Execution Flow Deposits Example: Aave Yield Hook - : Supplies new deposit to Aave (receives aToken) - Aave hook manages aToken balance as part of reserves - Coverage haircut naturally applies to aToken positions Withdrawals Swaps Example: Multi-Hook Swap - USDC hook (Aave): preSwap withdraws from Aave, postSwap re-deposits excess - WETH hook (Whitelist): preSwap checks sender, postSwap updates position tracking Flash Loans Hook Implementation Examples Base Hook Template All hooks should inherit from a base contract that implements the pool interface: Example 1: Aave Yield Optimization Automatically deposits reserves to Aave and withdraws when needed: Example 2: Whitelist with Position Limits Restrict deposits to whitelisted addresses with per-user position limits: Example 3: Deposit-Only Hook Demonstrate hook flags optimizationonly implement deposit hooks, all other hooks are no-ops: All other hooks automatically become no-ops due to flag checking in pool core: Hook Registration & Validation Registration Flow Validation Strategy Comprehensive one-time validation at registration (not runtime): 1. Code check: Ensure address has contract code (not EOA) 2. ERC-165 support: Verify returns true 3. Selector validation: Call all 12 hooks with dummy data, verify correct return values Benefits: - Zero runtime validation overhead (~2k gas saved per operation) - All hooks guaranteed compliant before use - Early detection of invalid hooks (rejected before use) - Owner can instantly replace hooks via Disabling Hooks To disable hooks for a token: Security Considerations Protected Against  Reentrancy: Hooks called within pool's context  Invalid Hooks: Comprehensive validation at registration (all 12 hooks tested)  Unauthorized Access: Hook contracts implement modifier  Bypass Attacks: Hook reverts cause full transaction revert  Upgrade Risks: Instant rollback possible via  Gas Griefing: No runtime validation (validated once at registration)  Return Value Attacks: Selector validation ensures correct return types Hook Access Control All hook contracts MUST implement access control: Without this, anyone could call hooks and manipulate pool state. Return Value Semantics Hooks must respect return value contracts: | Hook | Return Type | Purpose | |------|------------|---------| | | | Adjust final LP amount | | | | Adjust final withdrawal | | | | Modify swap fees | | | | Adjust pool reserves | | | | Bitmask of implemented hooks | | Other hooks | | No return value | Incorrect return values or types = hook will fail validation. Gas Costs | Operation | Hook Disabled | Hook Enabled (no-op) | Hook Enabled (Aave) | |-----------|---------------|----------------------|---------------------| | Deposit | ~100 gas | ~5,000 gas | ~55,000 gas | | Withdraw | ~100 gas | ~5,000 gas | ~60,000 gas | | Swap | ~200 gas | ~10,000 gas | ~110,000 gas | | Flash Loan | ~100 gas | ~5,000 gas | ~50,000 gas | Cost Breakdown - Disabled hooks: Just address check ( ) - Enabled hooks (no-op): Function call overhead (~5k gas) - Enabled hooks (real logic): Function call + custom logic (varies) - Registration: ~100-200k gas (one-time, validates all 12 hooks) Optimization Strategies 1. Hook Flags: Only set bits for hooks you actually use 2. Conditional Logic: Route per-token inside single hook 3. Selective Token Hooks: Disable hooks on low-value tokens Best Practices 1. Hook Design - Single Responsibility: One hook contract per use case - Token-Centric Routing: Handle multiple tokens inside single hook - Minimal Return Values: Only return non-zero for necessary adjustments 2. Integration - Pre-Hook Validation: Validate state before core operation - Post-Hook Adjustment: Modify results after core operation - Error Handling: Let hook reverts propagate (fail-safe model) 3. Testing - [ ] Deploy hook with desired configuration - [ ] Test each hook independently with dummy data - [ ] Test hook registration validation - [ ] Test hook disable and re-enable - [ ] Profile gas costs (enabled vs disabled) - [ ] Test per-token routing if applicable - [ ] Test return value semantics - [ ] Test reentrancy protection - [ ] Verify access control (onlyPool modifier) 4. Maintenance - Version Control: Tag hook versions (v1, v2, etc.) - Deployment Records: Keep audit trail of hook updates - Instant Rollback: Keep old hook contract deployed for quick revert Troubleshooting | Problem | Diagnosis | Solution | |---------|-----------|----------| | Hook not being called | Check has bit set | Set correct bit for hook | | Hook returns wrong type | Return value mismatch | Verify return type matches interface | | Hook reverts on valid input | Logic error in hook | Debug hook contract in isolation | | High gas on operations | Hook doing too much work | Profile hook execution, optimize | | Can't update hook | Validation failed | Ensure hook implements all 12 functions with correct selectors | Summary The Pool Hooks System combines:  Per-Token Customization - Finest granularity (one hook per asset)  Runtime Updateability - Swap hook contracts without liquidity migration  Gas Efficiency - Flag-based execution, ~100 gas when disabled  Type Safety - ERC-165 interface detection, selector validation  Security - One-time registration validation, zero runtime overhead  Simplicity - Direct calls, clear pool-perspective semantics Best For: Protocols needing per-token custom logic (yield optimization, access control, dynamic fees) with ability to upgrade over time. Key Files & References | File | Purpose | |------|---------| | | IPoolHooks interface definition | | | Hook flag constants | | | helper for flag checking | | | Hook execution in deposits, withdrawals, swaps | | | Example hook implementations | Version: 1.0 Last Updated: 2025-01-11
