documents.title: 2.4. Liquid Staking
documents.content: Liquid Staking Governance token and LP token staking with voting power, rewards, and timelocked exit 1. Overview Liquid staking in AIMM enables users to: - Lock BTR to earn voting power (sBTR receipt token) - Delegate voting rights to governance participants - Earn staking rewards from emissions pool (5% of total emissions) - Stake LP tokens to be eligible for liquidity provider rewards (90% of emissions) - Manage cooldowns on unstaking to prevent flash-loan voting attacks The system uses receipt tokens (sBTR for BTR, sLP per pool for LP tokens) to represent staked positions, enabling delegation and clear accounting. 2. BTR Staking (sBTR) 2.1. Staking Mechanics Stake action: Receipt token (sBTR): - ERC-20 token representing staked BTR - Fully transferable and fungible (major differentiator vs veCRV/veAERO) - Can be delegated, traded on DEXs, or used in other DeFi protocols - Accumulates staking rewards (rebase mechanism optional) - Voting power determinant at governance snapshot block Key differentiator: Unlike veCRV (non-transferable) or veAERO (NFT, non-fungible), sBTR is a standard ERC-20 that can be freely transferred. See BTR Token §4.1 for comparison. 2.2. Rewards & APR Reward source: 5% of total emissions (3.25M BTR over 10 years) Distribution mechanism: - Accumulator pattern (O(1) per claim): Similar to Aave's reward system - Per-block minting: Emissions accrued continuously, claimed on-demand - Pro-rata distribution: APR = (Annual emissions × 5%) / (Total sBTR market cap) Example APR calculation (Year 1): Claim frequency: Users can claim anytime (no minimum lock period after initial stake) 2.3. Voting Power Derivation sBTR holders' voting power is calculated at governance snapshot block: NB: This is the linear component. For complete formula including quadratic damping, see DAO Voting §2.2-2.3. Delegation: All voting power delegates to specified address for snapshot voting. Revoked via: 3. LP Token Staking (sLP) 3.1. Staking LP Tokens Each AIMM pool has an associated LP token (ERC-20, minted on deposit). Stake action (per pool): sLP properties: - One sLP token per pool (e.g., sLPETH/USDC, sLPWBTC/USDC) - Represents staked LP position, accrues rewards - Fully transferable and fungible (like sBTR — a key differentiator vs competitors) - Can be delegated, traded, or used as collateral in other protocols - Non-rebasing (balances don't change, only value increases via reward accumulation) - Bridgeable cross-chain via (see BridgeV1.sol) 3.2. Liquidity Provider Rewards Reward source: 90% of total emissions (58.5M BTR over 10 years) Allocation formula (per pool, per asset): Coverage weighting (see Inventory Management §2): - 100% coverage: 1.0x weight (ideal) - 100% coverage: Reduced weight (less risk = lower incentive) Utilization weighting: - Low utilization (0-20%): Reduced weight - Optimal utilization (50-80%): Maximum weight (1.0x) - High utilization (> 90%): Reduced weight (risk management) Claim frequency: Same as BTR staking (accumulator pattern, on-demand claims) 3.3. Multi-Pool LP Staking Users can stake LP tokens from multiple pools simultaneously: Each pool's emissions are independent (no competition between pools). 4. Unstaking & Cooldowns 4.1. Unstaking Mechanics Unstake action (burns receipt token): Two-phase process: 1. Request unstake (immediate): - User calls in staking module - Receipt tokens burned, cooldown timer starts - User cannot use these tokens during cooldown 2. Execute unstake (after cooldown): - User calls after cooldown period expires - Underlying tokens transferred to user - Cooldown timer cleared Cooldown duration: 2 weeks (configurable by governance) 4.2. Rationale for Cooldowns Flash-loan attack prevention: - Users can't stake in block N, vote in block N+1, unstake in block N+2 - Cooldown ensures committed participation (can't exit before vote execution) Governance finality: - Vote passes → 7-day timelock → Execution - Cooldown ensures users who voted remain exposed to consequences 4.3. Pending Unstakes Users can have multiple pending unstakes (e.g., unstake 10 sBTR on day 1, unstake 20 more on day 5): Each unstake is tracked separately and matures independently. 5. Staking Rewards Mechanics 5.1. Accumulator Pattern Reward accrual (O(1) per user): Benefits: - Gas-efficient: O(1) per claim, not O(N) iterations - Scalable: Works with millions of stakers - No staking order dependency 5.2. Claiming Rewards Users can claim accrued rewards anytime: Automatic reinvestment (optional): - Users can configure auto-claim → auto-stake - Rewards automatically reinvested into staking (compounding) - Useful for long-term holders 5.3. Reward Vesting sBTR staking rewards: Immediately claimable (no vesting) LP rewards: Governance-configurable: - Option A: Immediately claimable (standard) - Option B: Vesting period (e.g., 3-month linear, discourages short-term farming) 6. Delegation & Governance 6.1. Vote Delegation sBTR delegation: Effect on voting power: - Delegatee receives full voting power from delegator's sBTR balance - At governance snapshot, voting power calculated for delegatee - Delegator cannot vote if they've delegated (all power goes to delegatee) Multi-delegation: Not supported (each user has 1 delegatee) Revocation: Revocation effective immediately (next governance snapshot includes self-delegation) 6.2. Voting Power with Staking Voting power combines multiple components: For complete formula including quadratic damping, see DAO Voting §2.2-2.3. Boost incentive: Encourages users to both stake governance token AND provide liquidity 7. Advanced Staking Features 7.1. Auto-Staking for Vested Tokens Team members receiving vested BTR can configure: Effect: - Claimed vested BTR automatically staked into sBTR - User receives sBTR directly (not intermediate BTR) - sBTR eligible for voting power and staking rewards immediately Benefits: Team alignment (earning same rewards as community stakers) 7.2. Governance Parameter Adjustments Staking parameters adjustable via governance: | Parameter | Current | Min | Max | Type | |-----------|---------|-----|-----|------| | sBTR APR floor | 5% of emissions | 2% | 10% | Governance | | LP APR floor | 90% of emissions | 80% | 95% | Governance | | Cooldown duration | 2 weeks | 1 week | 4 weeks | Governance | | Max sLP per pool | Unlimited | — | — | Risk management | 8. Code References 8.1. Staking Module Contract: (interface: ) Key functions: - — Stake BTR, receive sBTR - — Request unstake, starts cooldown - — Finalize unstake after cooldown, receive BTR - — Claim accrued sBTR rewards - — Delegate voting power 8.2. LP Staking Interface: - — Stake LP token for specific pool - — Request unstake - — Finalize unstake 8.3. Reward Calculations Location: Reference implementation for: - Voting power aggregation across sBTR + sLP - Quadratic damping for large holders - Cross-chain aggregation 9. Security Considerations 9.1. Flash-Loan Safety Cooldown prevents: - Stake → Vote → Unstake in same block - Using borrowed funds to artificially inflate voting power - Flash-loan governance attacks Timing guarantee: - Snapshot block is in the past (no current-block voting) - Cooldown means even if unstake is ready, funds still need 2-week commitment 9.2. Delegation Risks Delegated voting risk: - Delegates have temporary control of voting power - If delegatee is compromised, voting power is compromised - Users can revoke anytime (no timelock on revocation) Mitigation: - Delegate only to trusted entities - Monitor voting history of delegates - Revoke if delegate behavior is suspicious 9.3. Smart Contract Risks - Staking contract audited by professional firm (pre-launch) - Emergency pause available if vulnerability discovered - Gradual rollout: Small initial cap, increase as confidence grows 10. documents.title: 3.2. Deployment & Upgrades
documents.content: Deployment & Upgradeability 1. Overview The protocol uses a modular diamond-lite proxy pattern for upgradeable pools and standalone contracts for treasury and bridge. This architecture balances upgradeability with security through timelocked governance. 2. Architecture 2.1. Core Components 1. PoolProxy ( ) - Lightweight EIP-2535-inspired proxy - Routes function calls to registered modules - ERC-7201 storage pattern for collision resistance - Immutable deployer for initialization security 2. Modules (Implementation contracts) - : Administrative functions - : Swap, deposit, withdraw logic - : Flash loan operations - : BTR and LP staking - : Reward distribution - : Price feed management 3. Standalone Contracts - : BTR token management, TGE, vesting - : Cross-chain token bridging 3. Deployment Process 3.1. Phase 1: Deploy Core Infrastructure 3.2. Phase 2: Deploy Pool via Factory Pattern 3.3. Phase 3: Connect Dependencies 4. Upgradeability Mechanisms 4.1. Module Upgrades Modules can be upgraded or replaced via HIGHTIMELOCK (3 days): Key Properties: - Selectors can point to different implementations - Multiple selectors can share one implementation - Init data allows constructor-like setup - Previous implementation remains unchanged 4.2. Storage Persistence All upgrades preserve storage via ERC-7201 namespaced storage: Guarantees: - Storage layout preserved across upgrades - No storage collision between modules - Standard ERC-7201 pattern 4.3. Adding New Functions New functionality can be added without affecting existing functions: 4.4. Removing Functions Selectors can be unregistered by pointing them to : 5. Non-Upgradeable Components The following components are immutable by design: 1. PoolProxy Fallback Logic - Selector routing is hardcoded - Only module addresses can change - Prevents rug-pull attacks 2. Treasury Contract - Cannot be upgraded - Ownership transferrable only - Protects vesting schedules 3. Bridge Contract - Cannot be upgraded - Migration requires new deployment - Rate limits protect against exploits 4. ERC-7201 Storage Locations - Hardcoded constants - Ensures storage safety 6. Security Through Timelocks All dangerous operations require time delays: CRITICAL | Operation | Timelock | Grace Period | Bypass | |-----------|----------|--------------|--------| | Base token migration | 7 days | 7 days | No | HIGH RISK | Ownership transfer | 3 days | 7 days | No | | Module update | 3 days | 7 days | No | | Bridge address update | 3 days | 7 days | No | | Treasury address update | 3 days | 7 days | No | MEDIUM RISK | Oracle config change | 2 days | 7 days | No | | Staking params update | 2 days | 7 days | No | | Distribution params | 2 days | 7 days | No | | Bridge peer config | 2 days | 3 days | No | | Bridge token config | 2 days | 3 days | No | LOW RISK | Add asset | 1 day | 7 days | No | | Update risk config | 1 day | 7 days | No | | Update fee params | 1 day | 7 days | No | EMERGENCY | Freeze asset | None | N/A | N/A | | Pause staking | None | N/A | N/A | | Pause bridge token | None | N/A | N/A | 6.1. Timelock Mechanics Grace Period Protection: - Operations expire after - Prevents indefinite pending operations - Requires re-initiation if expired 7. Deployment Configurations 7.1. Mainnet Deployment Treasury Owner: 3-of-5 Governance Multisig - Core team members initially - Transition to elected DAO council Bridge Owner: 3-of-5 DAO Council Multisig - Same signers as governance initially - Separate keys long-term Pool Owner (Official Pools): 3-of-5 DAO Council Multisig - Controls core protocol pools - Sets asset listings, risk params Pool Owner (Permissionless): Any address - Users can deploy their own pools - Full control over their pool - No protocol control 7.2. Testnet Deployment Shorter timelocks for testing: - CRITICAL: 1 hour - HIGH: 30 minutes - MEDIUM: 15 minutes - LOW: 5 minutes Not recommended for production value. 8. Permissionless Pool Deployment Anyone can deploy a pool via factory pattern: Properties: - Full control over your pool - No protocol governance - Timelocks still enforced (protects users) - Can use own oracles - Can set own fee parameters Recommended: - Use internal oracles only (Curve-style TWAPs) - Avoid external oracle dependencies - Set conservative risk parameters - Test thoroughly on testnet 9. Best Practices 9.1. For Module Developers 1. Never modify storage layout - Only append new storage variables - Use ERC-7201 namespaced slots - Document storage in comments 2. Use initialization functions - Not constructors (delegatecall context) - Include in module updates - Check initialization state 3. Maintain interface compatibility - Don't change function signatures - Add new functions, don't modify existing - Use versioned interfaces 4. Test with actual proxy - Don't test implementation directly - Use full deployment setup - Test upgrade paths 9.2. For Pool Operators 1. Use multisig for ownership - Minimum 3-of-5 signers - Distributed key custody - Hardware wallet signing 2. Announce changes in advance - Post to governance forum - Allow community review - Explain rationale 3. Test on staging first - Deploy to testnet - Run full scenarios - Monitor for issues 4. Monitor post-upgrade - Watch events - Check state consistency - Have rollback plan 9.3. For Users 1. Verify module addresses - Check on-chain via - Compare against official deployments - Use block explorers 2. Monitor timelock events - Subscribe to - Review pending operations - Exit if suspicious 3. Understand risks - Upgradeable pools have governance risk - Timelocks provide exit window - Emergency freezes possible 10. Emergency Procedures 10.1. Asset Freeze (No Timelock) Effect: Disables swap, deposit, withdraw, flash loans immediately. 10.2. Staking Pause (No Timelock) Effect: Disables stake/unstake while allowing reward claims. 10.3. Bridge Token Pause (No Timelock) Effect**: Prevents inbound and outbound bridging immediately. 11. Upgrade Checklist Before deploying an upgrade: - [ ] Storage layout unchanged or safely extended - [ ] All selectors mapped correctly - [ ] Initialization data prepared - [ ] Timelock announced to community - [ ] Testnet upgrade successful - [ ] Security audit completed (for major changes) - [ ] Emergency freeze procedures documented - [ ] Monitoring alerts configured - [ ] Rollback plan documented

documents.title: 3.5. Oracles
documents.content: Oracle System Multi-timeframe TWAP and volatility tracking for informed pricing 1. Overview AIMM uses a two-oracle pattern: 1. Internal Oracle (InternalOracleV1) — Auto-updated on every swap, tracks TWAPs and volatility from execution prices 2. External Oracle (ExternalOracle) — Push-based feeds from Chainlink, Pyth, or custom keepers The system decouples price discovery from reserves, enabling informed market making instead of mechanical invariant pricing. 2. Internal Oracle (InternalOracleV1) 2.1. Purpose Tracks pool-observed prices with dual-timeframe smoothing: - Fast TWAP: 5-minute window (responsive to recent trades) - Slow TWAP: 1-hour window (resistant to manipulation) Both TWAPs update automatically after each swap — no external keeper required. 2.2. Feed Structure Storage per token (spans multiple slots): 2.3. Accumulator Decimals (accDecimals) The parameter controls how TWAP accumulators are encoded in B64 format. Using lower decimals provides more headroom for time-weighted accumulation: | Asset Class | Example | accDecimals | Max Accumulator | Practical Limit | |-------------|---------|-------------|-----------------|-----------------| | Stablecoins | USDC, USDT | 6 | ~4.5×10⁷² | >10,000 years | | Mid-cap | ETH, SOL | 12 | ~4.5×10⁶⁶ | >10,000 years | | High-value | BTC, WBTC | 18 | ~4.5×10⁶⁰ | >1,000 years | Why this matters: B64 float format has 52-bit mantissa with exponent range ±63. The accumulator stores: For stablecoins (~$1), using : - Price in accDecimals base: ≈ 1×10⁶ - After 1 year: 1×10⁶ × 31.5M seconds ≈ 3×10¹³ - B64 mantissa max: ~4.5×10¹⁵ (plenty of room before exponent kicks in) - With exponent: can handle up to ~4.5×10⁷² For BTC (~$100k), using : - Price in accDecimals base: ≈ 1×10²³ - After 1 year: 1×10²³ × 31.5M ≈ 3×10³⁰ - Still within B64 range (~4.5×10⁶⁰) Configuration: Set via when adding assets: Default is if not specified (stablecoin-optimized). 2.4. Constants | Constant | Value | Description | |----------|-------|-------------| | | 300s | 5-minute TWAP window | | | 3600s | 1-hour TWAP window | | | 200 | 0.02% volatility smoothing | | | 1800 | 0.18% volatility smoothing | | | 100,000,000 | 10,000% max vol (1e6 base) | | | 3600 | 1 hour staleness threshold | 2.5. Update Flow On every swap, is called: 2.5.1. Logic 1. Same-block protection: Skip if (prevents manipulation) 2. Accumulator update (using accDecimals, not token decimals): 3. Fast TWAP (every 5 minutes): 4. Slow TWAP (every hour): 5. Volatility EMA: 2.6. Offset Encoding Offsets represent TWAP deviation from spot price: Decoding (in LibOracle): Benefits: - Single B64 decode per price read - Offsets applied in 1e18 space (no redundant encoding) - int32 range covers ±214,748% deviation 3. External Oracle (ExternalOracle) 3.1. Purpose Push-based oracle for: - Chainlink/Pyth price feeds - Off-chain keeper updates - Cross-chain price aggregation 3.2. Feed Structure Same struct as internal oracle: 3.3. Feed Management Adding a feed: Feed ID: Pushing updates: 3.4. Access Control | Role | Capabilities | |------|--------------| | Owner | Add feeds, update config, grant/revoke oracles | | Oracle | Push price updates | 4. B64 Float Encoding 4.1. Format (52/5/7) | Field | Bits | Range | Description | |-------|------|-------|-------------| | Mantissa | 52 | 0 - 4.5×10^15 | Normalized value | | Decimals | 5 | 0-31 | Token decimal places | | Exponent | 7 | -64 to +63 (biased by 64) | Scale factor | 4.2. Encoding (LibMaths) 1. Normalize mantissa to 52 bits 2. Compute exponent from normalization shift 3. Pack: 4.3. Decoding (LibMaths) 1. Extract mantissa, decimals, exponent 2. Compute total shift = exponent - bias + decimals 3. Return: (normalized to 1e18) 4.4. Example Price: 2500.00 USDC (6 decimals) - Value: 2,500,000,000 (2500 × 10^6) - Mantissa: Normalized to 52 bits - Decimals: 6 - Exponent: Based on normalization 5. LibOracle Functions 5.1. Price Decoding 5.2. Volatility & Deviation 5.3. Base Token Feed Returns: - : 1.0 encoded - Offsets: 0 - Volatility: 0.01% baseline - TTL: Never expires 6. Oracle Selection 6.1. Mode Flags Configured per asset in : | Mode Flag | Bit | Behavior | |-----------|-----|----------| | | 0x01 | Prefer internal oracle | | | 0x02 | Prefer external oracle | | | 0x04 | Fall back to secondary on stale/missing | 6.2. Selection Logic 7. Transient Caching (EIP-1153) For gas optimization, caches decoded prices in transient storage: Savings: ~2,100 gas per cache hit Scope: Single transaction (clears automatically) 8. Security Considerations 8.1. Manipulation Resistance 1. Same-block skip: Prevents multiple updates in one block 2. TWAP smoothing: 5min/1hr windows resist flash loan manipulation 3. Dual-window cross-check: Large fast/slow divergence triggers higher fees 8.2. Staleness Protection 1. TTL enforcement: Feeds expire after configurable period 2. Confidence scoring: External feeds can signal uncertainty 3. Fallback cascade: Secondary oracle protects against primary failure 8.3. Deviation Bounds 1. maxDeviation threshold: Rejects external pushes with extreme moves 2. MAXVOLATILITY cap: 10,000% ceiling prevents overflow 3. Offset clamping: int32 range prevents extreme TWAP divergence 9. Usage Examples 9.1. Reading Internal Oracle 9.2. Initializing Oracle Note:** determines accumulator range vs precision tradeoff. Lower values = more headroom for long-running pools. See Accumulator Decimals section. 9.3. External Oracle Push 10. documents.title: 3.4. Flow Guards
documents.content: 3.4. Flow Guards (Reentrancy & MEV Protection) Multi-layered temporal protection against callback, reentrancy, and JIT manipulation attacks Overview The Flow Guard System is a two-layer security architecture that protects against malicious interaction flows at different attack levels: | Layer | Mechanism | Scope | Attack Vector | Implementation | |-------|-----------|-------|----------------|-----------------| | L1: Transaction Level | Reentrancy Guard | Same transaction | Callback-based reentrancy | EIP-1153 transient storage | | L2: Block Level | Time-Based Flow Guard | Cross-transaction | JIT liquidity / MEV bundles | Timestamped cooldowns | Both layers work together to create a defense-in-depth strategy against flow manipulation: Layer 1: Reentrancy Guard (Transaction-Level) What It Protects Against Reentrancy is when an external contract calls back into the pool during the execution of an operation, before that operation completes. Attack Example: Implementation (EIP-1153) The pool uses EIP-1153 transient storage for reentrancy protection: Key Properties: - Transient Storage (TLOAD/TSTORE): Data cleared at end of transaction - Zero Cost on revert: Transient storage is automatically cleaned up - Simple: Single locked/unlocked flag - Fast: ~100 gas (vs ~20k for sstore) Protected Operations All user-facing pool operations are wrapped: - - prevents callback during transfer - - prevents callback during transfer - - prevents callback during swaps - , , etc. - all external calls protected What Reentrancy Guard Does NOT Prevent Same-block attacks that don't use callbacks: - JIT liquidity bundles (Flashbots ordering) - Multi-transaction atomic sequences in same block - MEV sandwich attacks - Price oracle staleness attacks These require Layer 2 (Flow Guard) protection. Layer 2: Flow Guard (Block-Level MEV Protection) What It Protects Against JIT (Just-In-Time) Liquidity is an MEV strategy where sophisticated actors: 1. Observe a pending large swap in the mempool 2. Deposit liquidity in the same block (via Flashbots bundle) 3. Capture swap fees from the large trade 4. Withdraw liquidity in the same block (atomic) This extracts value that should go to long-term LPs, without bearing any price risk. Research Context: - JIT attacks account for ~0.5-1% of Uniswap v3 volume - Dominated by 3-5 sophisticated MEV bots - Average extraction: 5-15 bps per targeted swap - Long-term LPs lose fee income to zero-risk extractors Protected Flows | Flow | Entry Action | Exit Action | Protection | Use Case | |------|--------------|-------------|-----------|----------| | Deposit→Withdraw | | , | 15s cooldown | Prevents JIT LP positioning | | Stake Gov→Unstake Gov | | | 15s cooldown | Prevents instant voting/reward capture | | Stake LP→Unstake LP | | | 15s cooldown | Prevents JIT reward farming | Example Attack Timeline: How Time-Based Flow Guard Works Architecture Operation Flow Time-Based (Not Block-Based) The cooldown is measured in seconds, not blocks. This ensures: - Consistent protection across all EVM chains - Works on chains with variable block times (Arbitrum, Polygon, etc.) - Protection scales with real-world time, not validator behavior Configuration Default Value The 15-second default was chosen because: - Long enough to span multiple blocks on any major EVM chain - Short enough to not impede legitimate users - Practical for cross-chain consistency Admin Control Pool owners can adjust the cooldown: NB: Setting completely disables the flow guard. Maximum Value The type allows up to 65,535 seconds (~18.2 hours). Values above 300 seconds (5 minutes) are generally impractical. Error Handling When a cooldown violation is detected: Example: - User deposits at T=100 - User tries to withdraw at T=105 (cooldown=15s) - Reverts with (10 seconds remaining) Defense-in-Depth Architecture Attack Surface Coverage The two-layer system protects against different attack surfaces: L1 vs L2 Comparison | Property | Reentrancy Guard (L1) | Flow Guard (L2) | |----------|----------------------|-----------------| | Scope | Same transaction | Cross-transaction | | Duration | Single function call | 15 seconds | | Attack Vector | Callback reentrancy | JIT liquidity / MEV | | Implementation | TLOAD/TSTORE flag | Timestamp cooldowns | | Gas Cost | ~100 gas | ~5-7k gas per operation | | Frequency | Every operation | Entry + exit check | Attack Timeline Example Reentrancy Attack (L1): JIT Liquidity Attack (L2): Why Both Layers Matter - Layer 1 alone (just reentrancy guard): Stops callback attacks but not MEV bundles - Layer 2 alone (just flow guard): Stops JIT attacks but not malicious callbacks - Both layers (defense-in-depth): Comprehensive protection against flow manipulation Example: If Layer 1 didn't exist, a malicious token could: 1. User calls 2. Pool transfers 1000 tokens 3. Token's fallback calls on pool 4. Withdrawal succeeds during deposit → potential theft This attack is prevented by Layer 1's reentrancy guard. Stake Lock Duration Staking already has a (default 14 days) that prevents unstaking for a period. Flow Guard adds an additional entry-side protection: - Stake Lock: Prevents early unstake regardless of entry timing - Flow Guard: Prevents immediate unstake after stake (JIT reward capture) A user who stakes must wait: 1. (15s) before they can even attempt to unstake 2. (14 days) before the stake is actually unlocked Combined Protection Model How Layers Interact Both reentrancy guard and flow guard are applied to complementary operations: Sequential Protection User flow is protected at both levels: What About Both Attacks Simultaneously? A sophisticated attacker might try to combine strategies: Even if Layer 1 didn't exist, Layer 2 would still prevent the JIT attack. Even if Layer 2 didn't exist, Layer 1 would still prevent the callback attack. Result: Two independent, complementary defenses. Implementation Details Layer 1: Reentrancy Guard Storage (Transient) Reentrancy guard uses EIP-1153 transient storage (TLOAD/TSTORE): Transient Storage Advantages: - Data lives only for one transaction - Automatically cleaned up at end of transaction - No gas refunds needed - Fast access (~100 gas vs ~20k for persistent storage) - Perfect for mutex flags Layer 2: Flow Guard Storage (Persistent) Flow guard uses standard persistent storage with ERC-7201 namespace: Storage Design: - Three separate timestamp mappings for three flow types - timestamps (good until year 2106) - Namespace prevents collision with other pools/contracts - Persistent storage needed to track across transactions Gas Costs Layer 1: Reentrancy Guard | Operation | Gas Cost | Note | |-----------|----------|------| | Entry (TSTORE 1) | ~100 | Transient storage write | | Exit (TSTORE 0) | ~100 | Transient storage clear | | Revert check (TLOAD) | ~100 | Read on reentry attempt | | Total per operation | ~100-200 | Applied to ALL external calls | Layer 2: Flow Guard | Operation | Gas Cost | Context | |-----------|----------|---------| | Record timestamp (deposit) | ~5,000 | SSTORE to cold slot (first time) | | Record timestamp (stake) | ~5,000 | SSTORE to cold slot (first time) | | Check cooldown (withdraw) | ~2,100 | SLOAD from slot (already warm) | | Check cooldown (unstake) | ~2,100 | SLOAD from slot (already warm) | Combined Overhead | Operation | L1 | L2 | Total | |-----------|----|----|-------| | (write timestamp) | 100 | 5,000 | ~5,100 | | (check cooldown) | 100 | 2,100 | ~2,200 | | (no flow guard) | 100 | 0 | ~100 | Context: - A typical deposit costs ~100-200k gas - Flow guard adds ~2-5% overhead - Reentrancy guard adds <1% overhead - Combined overhead is small relative to operation cost Optimization note: After first warm-up, subsequent operations on same storage slot cost less due to "warm" slot pricing (100 gas vs 2,100 gas). What Flow Guards Does NOT Protect Against Layer 1 Limitations (Reentrancy Guard) Reentrancy guard only protects against callback-based attacks: 1. Multi-step attacks - Attacks that require user interaction outside the callback (e.g., "step 1: transfer out, step 2: user action, step 3: callback") 2. Cross-contract reentrancy - If the pool calls Contract A, which calls Contract B, which calls back into pool (needs more sophisticated analysis) Layer 2 Limitations (Time-Based Flow Guard) Flow guard does not protect against: 1. Long-term statistical arbitrage - If someone deposits for 1 day, they still capture fees during that time 2. Information-based trading - Traders with alpha about future prices (this is not MEV extraction) 3. Cross-pool attacks - Coordination across multiple pools 4. Off-chain coordination - Multiple wallets controlled by same entity 5. Oracle manipulation - Price feed attacks (separate concern, handled by oracle layer) Complementary Defenses Both flow guards are one layer in a comprehensive defense-in-depth strategy: | Layer | Mechanism | Prevents | |-------|-----------|----------| | L1: Reentrancy | Transient storage flag | Callback attacks during operation | | L2: Flow Guard | Timestamped cooldowns | JIT liquidity and MEV bundling | | L3: Pricing | Directional fees | Toxic/coverage-worsening trades | | L4: Oracle | TWAP + staleness checks | Price feed manipulation | | L5: Volatility | Spread adjustment | Exploitation during uncertainty | Example: A complete attack chain might involve: 1. Oracle manipulation (L4 blocks) 2. Attempt to exploit pricing (L3 charges premium) 3. JIT deposit-and-swap (L2 blocks) 4. Malicious callback (L1 blocks) Each layer independently protects, and combined they create comprehensive security. Summary: Two-Layer Flow Protection The Flow Guard System consolidates two complementary security mechanisms into a unified architecture: Layer 1: Reentrancy Guard (Transaction-Level) - Scope: Same transaction - Protection: Callback-based reentrancy attacks - Implementation: EIP-1153 transient storage flag - Cost: ~100 gas per operation - Applies to: All external calls (deposit, withdraw, swap, stake, etc.) Layer 2: Time-Based Flow Guard (Block-Level) - Scope: Cross-transaction (15-second default cooldown) - Protection: JIT liquidity and MEV bundling attacks - Implementation: Timestamped cooldowns on complementary operations - Cost: ~5k gas on entry, ~2.1k gas on exit - Applies to: Deposit→withdraw, stake→unstake flows Design Principles 1. Defense-in-Depth: Both layers work independently - Layer 1 alone stops callback attacks - Layer 2 alone stops JIT attacks - Combined = comprehensive protection 2. Low Gas Overhead - Reentrancy: <1% of operation cost - Flow guard: 2-5% of operation cost - Minimal friction for users 3. Per-Transaction Clarity - Layer 1 clears automatically at end of transaction - Layer 2 persists across transactions - No manual cleanup needed 4. Simple, Auditable Code - Single flag per transaction (Layer 1) - Three timestamp mappings (Layer 2) - No complex state machines Key Takeaway The two layers protect different attack surfaces: - Reentrancy Guard: "Can you call back into us during our operation?" - Answer: No, flag prevents it - Flow Guard: "Can you deposit and withdraw atomically in the same block?" - Answer: No, 15-second cooldown prevents it Together, they form a robust defense against the most common flow manipulation attacks on AMMs. Related Documentation - 3.1. Security Overview - 1.2.4. Spread & Fees - 1.2.6. Anti-Toxic Flow Protection

documents.title: Overview
documents.content: Security Overview Defense-in-depth architecture for AIMM protocol security 1. Security Philosophy AIMM employs a defense-in-depth approach with multiple independent security layers: 1. Economic Security  Incentive alignment and manipulation resistance 2. Access Control  Timelocked governance and role separation 3. Operational Security  Circuit breakers and emergency controls 4. Code Security  Audits, testing, and formal verification 2. Threat Model 2.1. Adversary Capabilities | Adversary | Capabilities | Mitigations | |-----------|--------------|-------------| | Flash Loan Attacker | Unlimited capital for single transaction | Same-block oracle rejection, TWAP pricing | | Whale Trader | Large positions, multi-block attacks | Dual-window TWAPs, inventory skew bounds | | MEV Searcher | Transaction ordering, sandwich attacks | Slippage protection, directional fees | | Oracle Manipulator | External feed compromise | Dual oracle, deviation detection | | Governance Attacker | Majority token control | Timelocks, grace periods | | Smart Contract Exploiter | Code vulnerability discovery | Audits, bug bounties, upgradability | 2.2. Trust Assumptions | Component | Trust Level | Justification | |-----------|-------------|---------------| | Owner | Trusted | Multi-sig with timelock | | Treasury | Trusted | Fee collection only | | Bridge | Semi-trusted | Limited to mint/burn operations | | External Oracles | Verified | Deviation checking, fallbacks | | Users | Untrusted | All inputs validated | 3. Security Layers 3.1. Layer 1: Economic Security Manipulation Resistance: - Dual TWAP Windows  5-minute (fast) and 1-hour (slow) averages - Same-Block Rejection  Oracle updates skip same-block trades - Inventory Skew Bounds  Maximum ±100 skew caps price impact - Coverage Floor  50% minimum prevents complete drainage Incentive Alignment: - Directional Fees  Toxic flow pays higher spread - LP Haircuts  Undercollateralized withdrawals penalized - Decay Mechanism  Long-term undercollateralization resolved 3.2. Layer 2: Access Control Role Separation: | Role | Permissions | Holder | |------|-------------|--------| | Owner | All admin functions (timelocked) | Multi-sig wallet | | Treasury | Collect protocol fees | Treasury contract | | Bridge | Mint/burn for cross-chain | Bridge contract | | Oracles | Push price updates | Authorized keepers | Timelock Tiers: - CRITICAL (7 days)  Base token migration - HIGH (3 days)  Ownership, modules, treasury, bridge - BASE (2 days)  Oracle changes, staking config - LOW (1 day)  Add asset, fee updates Grace Period: 7 days to execute after timelock expires. 3.3. Layer 3: Operational Security Circuit Breakers: Emergency Controls: -  Immediate halt (no timelock) -  Restore operations - Per-asset granularity Thresholds: -  Minimum healthy coverage (default 50%) -  Decay activation threshold -  Reserve floor per asset 3.4. Layer 4: Code Security Development Practices: - Solidity 0.8.28 with overflow checks - Extensive natspec documentation - Custom error types (gas efficient) - Modular architecture (isolated concerns) Testing: - Unit tests for all functions - Integration tests for flows - Fuzz testing for edge cases - Invariant testing for properties External Review: - Third-party audits — Pre-launch security review by professional auditors 4. Storage Security 4.1. ERC-7201 Namespaced Storage Each module uses isolated storage slots: Benefits: - No slot collisions between modules - Safe upgrades without storage migration - Clear separation of concerns 4.2. Transient Storage (EIP-1153) Used for transaction-scoped data: - Reentrancy guards - Oracle price caching - Flash loan state Security Properties: - Auto-cleared after transaction - Cannot persist malicious state - Gas efficient 5. Reentrancy Protection 5.1. Transient Guard Pattern Protected Operations: - All external token transfers - Flash loan callbacks - Cross-module calls 6. Oracle Security 6.1. Internal Oracle Manipulation Resistance: | Attack | Defense | |--------|---------| | Flash loan | Same-block rejection | | Multi-block | Dual-window TWAP | | Low liquidity | External fallback | | Staleness | TTL-based freshness check | 6.2. External Oracle Validation: - Deviation bounds checking - Staleness detection - Multi-source aggregation option Fallback Chain: See: Oracles 7. Upgrade Security 7.1. Diamond-Lite Proxy Module Registry: Upgrade Process: 1. Request module update (3-day timelock) 2. Wait for delay 3. Execute within 7-day grace 4. Old module removed, new module active Immutable Components: - Proxy contract itself - Storage slot locations - Core libraries See: Deployment & Upgrades 8. Emergency Procedures 8.1. Security Incident Response Phase 1: Immediate (0-1 hour) 1. Identify affected assets 2. Execute on affected tokens 3. Alert team and security partners 4. Begin investigation Phase 2: Assessment (1-24 hours) 1. Determine root cause 2. Assess damage extent 3. Identify fix requirements 4. Prepare communication Phase 3: Remediation (1-7+ days) 1. Develop and test fix 2. Submit timelocked upgrade 3. Coordinate disclosure 4. Execute fix after delay Phase 4: Recovery 1. Unfreeze assets 2. Monitor closely 3. Post-mortem analysis 4. Update procedures 8.2. Contact Information For security disclosures: - Security email: sec@btr.supply - Response SLA: 24 hours 9. Known Limitations 9.1. Economic Bounds | Limitation | Bound | Implication | |------------|-------|-------------| | Max skew | ±100 | ~100% premium/discount at extremes | | Max depth | 4 levels | Complex routing limited | | Max hops | 6 | Long paths split execution | 9.2. Oracle Limitations | Limitation | Mitigation | |------------|------------| | Low volume  stale TWAP | External fallback, shorter TTL | | Fast price movement | Wider spreads via volatility | | External feed failure | Multi-source, internal fallback | 9.3. Governance Limitations | Limitation | Mitigation | |------------|------------| | Owner compromise | Timelock delays, multi-sig | | Slow emergency response | Immediate freeze (no timelock) | | Governance attack | Grace period limits exposure | 10. Security Checklist 10.1. For Pool Deployers - [ ] Multi-sig wallet for owner - [ ] Reasonable initial parameters - [ ] External oracle fallback configured - [ ] Emergency contacts established - [ ] Monitoring systems active 10.2. For LPs - [ ] Understand coverage mechanics - [ ] Monitor coverage ratios - [ ] Understand withdrawal haircuts - [ ] Verify pool parameters 10.3. For Traders - [ ] Set appropriate slippage - [ ] Verify pool coverage - [ ] Check oracle freshness - [ ] Understand fee structure 11. Related Documentation - Deployment & Upgrades — Upgrade procedures and deployment - Access Control — Roles and permissions - Flow Guards — JIT protection, cooldowns - Oracles — Oracle security and fallbacks - Admin Module — Administrative functions

documents.title: 3.3. Access Control
documents.content: Governance & Access Control 1. Overview The protocol implements a comprehensive governance system with role-based access control, timelocked operations, and emergency procedures. Governance uses a three-multisig architecture (Treasury, Admin/Council, Guardian) with transparent on-chain operations and community oversight via Snapshot voting. 2. Governance Entities 2.1. Treasury Multisig (Governance Multisig) Contract: at Initial Setup: 3-of-5 multisig (core team) Long-term: 3-of-5 elected DAO council Powers: - Mint BTR tokens to any address (immediate) - Grant vested allocations during TGE initialization - Allocate incentives to pool distributors - Mint BTR to distributor contracts - Distributors handle per-pool distribution - Special allocations for events, grants, partnerships - Direct minting to recipients - No vesting cliffs for special cases - Collect protocol fees from pools - Transfer ownership (7-day timelock) Cannot Do: - Burn tokens from other addresses - Modify vesting schedules post-TGE - Access pool governance functions - Control bridge operations 2.2. Bridge Owner (DAO Council) Contract: at Initial Setup: 3-of-5 multisig (core team) Long-term: 3-of-5 elected DAO council Powers: - Configure bridgeable tokens (2-day timelock) - Set cross-chain peers (2-day timelock) - Pause/unpause tokens (immediate) - Set daily bridge limits - Outbound: Absolute amount per token - Inbound: Percentage of outbound (e.g., 120%) - B64-encoded for gas efficiency - Migrate to new bridges - Deploy new bridge contract - Update token mint/burn permissions - Transition over grace period - Rescue stuck tokens (immediate) Cannot Do: - Mint tokens directly (only via ERC-7802 callbacks) - Bypass rate limits - Access pool or treasury functions 2.3. Pool Owner (Curator) Contract: Any instance Initial Setup: - Core Protocol Pools: 3-of-5 DAO council multisig - Permissionless Pools: Deployer's choice (any address) Long-term: - Official Pools: Elected DAO council - Permissionless Pools: Pool creator's discretion Powers: 2.3.1. Asset Management (1-day timelock) - Add assets to pool - Update risk configurations (1-day timelock) RiskConfig Parameters: - : FROZEN | SWAPENABLED | LIABILITYSWAPENABLED | DECAYENABLED | FLASHENABLED | FEEONTRANSFER | STAKEABLE | BRIDGEABLE - : Maximum liquidity profile depth - : Liability decay threshold - : Decay rate parameter - : Circuit breaker threshold - Update liquidity profiles (depth curve shapes) LiquidityProfile Structure: - : Price offset knots (int8, weights.length + 1 points) - : Liquidity weights per segment (uint8) - Total weights must sum to 200 - Knots must be monotonically increasing - max(knots) - min(knots) must equal 100 2.3.2. Oracle Management (2-day timelock) - Configure price oracles OracleConfig Parameters: - : Primary oracle address (or for internal) - : Fallback oracle address - : Price feed identifier - : USEINTERNAL | USEEXTERNAL | ALLOWFALLBACK - Update anchor relationships (immediate) Controls pricing topology in anchor tree architecture. 2.3.3. Fee Management (1-day timelock) - Update fee parameters 2.3.4. Staking Parameters (2-day timelock) - Update staking lock durations - Configure LP staking Deploys deterministic staked LP (sLP) token via CREATE3. - Pause/unpause staking (immediate) 2.3.5. Distribution Management (2-day timelock) - Add reward tokens - Set emission rates - Update claim parameters (2-day timelock) Parameters: - : Minimum reward multiplier without sBTR (basis points) - : sBTR value needed to match LP value for full rewards 2.3.6. Critical Operations (3-7 day timelock) - Transfer pool ownership (3-day timelock) - Update modules (3-day timelock) - Update bridge address (3-day timelock) - Update treasury address (3-day timelock) - Migrate base token (7-day timelock) 2.3.7. Emergency Powers (Immediate) - Freeze assets (no timelock) - Pause staking (no timelock) Cannot Do: - Mint BTR tokens - Control bridge operations - Access other pools' governance - Bypass timelocks (except emergency freezes) 2.4. External Oracle Keeper Role: Off-chain EOA or multisig Contracts: instances Initial Setup: Keeper EOA (can be upgraded to multisig) Long-term: Decentralized keeper network or DAO-controlled multisig Powers: - Push price feeds on-chain - Update multiple feeds (batch operation) Responsibilities: - Fetch prices from reliable off-chain sources - Calculate TWAP/EMA to prevent manipulation - Update at regular intervals (e.g., every 5 minutes) - Monitor for price anomalies - Maintain high uptime Security Requirements: - Use TWAP prices: Not spot prices (flash loan protection) - Multi-source aggregation: Combine multiple exchanges - Outlier detection: Reject suspicious price movements - Transparency: Public monitoring of price updates - Decentralization: Multiple keepers with rotation Critical Importance: External oracles are mission-critical for pools using them. Stale or manipulated prices can lead to: - Incorrect swap rates - Arbitrage exploitation - Insolvency risk - User losses Recommendation for Permissionless Pools: - Prefer internal oracles (Curve-style TWAPs) - Use external oracles only if: - Highly reputable (Chainlink, Pyth, etc.) - Multiple fallbacks configured - Circuit breakers enabled - You trust the keeper 3. Timelock Overview All timelocks follow this pattern: 1. Request: Owner initiates operation - Emits - Stores operation data on-chain 2. Wait: Time passes (1, 2, 3, or 7 days) - Users can review pending operations - Community can discuss in forum - Exit window for concerned users 3. Execute: Owner executes after timelock expires - Must be within grace period - Emits operation-specific event - Changes take effect 4. Cancel (optional): Owner cancels before execution - Emits - Clears pending operation 3.1. Timelock Summary Table | Risk Level | Delay | Operations | |------------|-------|------------| | Emergency | None | Freeze asset, pause staking, pause bridge token | | Low | 1 day | Add asset, update risk config, update fees | | Medium | 2 days | Oracle config, staking params, distribution params, bridge config | | High | 3 days | Ownership transfer, module update, bridge/treasury update | | Critical | 7 days | Base token migration, treasury ownership | Grace Periods: - Pool operations: 7 days - Bridge operations: 3 days - Treasury operations: 7 days 4. Multi-Signature Requirements All governance entities should use multisig wallets: 4.1. Recommended Setup (Launch) Governance Multisig (Treasury): - Threshold: 3-of-5 - Signers: Core team members - Key Storage: Hardware wallets (Ledger, Trezor) - Geographic Distribution: Different jurisdictions - Backup Plans: Key recovery procedures DAO Council Multisig (Bridge + Official Pools): - Threshold: 3-of-5 - Signers: Core team initially, elected members later - Key Storage: Hardware wallets - Geographic Distribution: Different jurisdictions - Meeting Cadence: Weekly sync calls 4.2. Long-Term Setup (Post-DAO) Elected Council: - Selection: Token-weighted voting - Term: 6-12 months - Accountability: On-chain voting records - Compensation: Protocol emissions - Removal: Governance vote if malicious 5. Emergency Procedures 5.1. Asset Exploitation Detected 1. Immediate: Freeze affected asset 2. Within 1 hour: Assess impact - Check reserves vs liabilities - Identify affected users - Estimate losses 3. Within 24 hours: Public disclosure - Post-mortem to governance forum - Explanation of freeze reason - Proposed remediation plan 4. Timelock: Update risk config or remove asset 5. After resolution: Unfreeze if safe 5.2. Bridge Exploit Detected 1. Immediate: Pause affected token 2. Coordinate: Contact other chain councils - Pause on all chains - Investigate root cause 3. If compromise is severe: Deploy new bridge - New contract deployment - Update token permissions - Migrate liquidity 5.3. Oracle Manipulation Detected 1. Immediate: Freeze assets using bad oracle 2. Switch to fallback: If available 3. Investigate: Oracle keeper - Check keeper signing keys - Review recent price updates - Identify manipulation method 4. Long-term: Replace keeper or switch to internal oracle 6. Governance Architecture 6.1. Off-Chain Voting with On-Chain Execution AIMM uses Snapshot-based governance rather than fully on-chain voting. This design choice is intentional: Why not on-chain governance? - Cross-chain compatibility — Voting power spans multiple chains (Ethereum, Arbitrum, Base, etc.) - Liquid staking — sBTR/sLP are transferable; on-chain voting would require lock mechanisms - Gas efficiency — Off-chain voting is free; on-chain proposals cost gas - UX simplicity — Snapshot provides a familiar, user-friendly interface Transparency guarantees: - All voting power derived from on-chain state at snapshot block - Multisig execution of approved proposals is publicly visible - Timelocks provide community exit opportunity - All parameters and operations logged on-chain For complete governance mechanics, see DAO Voting. 7. Access Control Architecture 7.1. Role Hierarchy 7.2. Permission Verification All privileged functions use the modifier: Treasury uses Solady's pattern for consistency. 8. Monitoring & Transparency 8.1. On-Chain Events All governance actions emit events for transparency: 8.2. Recommended Monitoring For Users: - Subscribe to events - Review pending operations via governance dashboard - Exit positions if suspicious changes proposed For Council Members: - Monitor oracle price updates - Track daily bridge volumes - Review protocol fee accumulation - Watch for emergency freezes For Developers: - Track module upgrades - Monitor storage layout changes - Test against staging deployments 9. Best Practices 9.1. For Governance Multisig Signers 1. Use hardware wallets: Never sign from hot wallets 2. Verify transactions: Double-check addresses and amounts 3. Communicate clearly: Discuss proposals before signing 4. Document decisions: Keep records of reasoning 5. Rotate keys: Periodically update signer set 9.2. For Pool Operators 1. Announce changes: Post to forum before timelock 2. Explain rationale: Why is change needed? 3. Test on testnet: Verify expected behavior 4. Monitor post-change: Watch for unexpected effects 5. Have rollback plan: Be ready to revert if needed 9.3. For Oracle Keepers 1. Use TWAP prices: Never push spot prices 2. Multi-source data: Aggregate multiple exchanges 3. Outlier detection: Reject suspicious prices 4. High uptime: Keep feed fresh (<5 min delay) 5. Transparency: Public monitoring dashboards
